Because $B\mathrm{O}$ and $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ are grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces,1414 14 It is not immediately obvious that $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ is a grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -space, but one can prove it by modifying the argument in [DY23a, Proof of Proposition 1.20]. one can prove the proposition by lifting the map $B\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ to the equivalent data of a map of spectra $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}\colon\mathit{bo}_{0}\to\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/\mathit{bstring}$ .1515 15 The name $\mathit{bo}_{0}$ instead of $\mathit{bo}$ is because it is traditional to use $\mathit{bo}$ to refer to the spectrum corresponding to the grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -space $\mathbb{Z}\times B\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. the spectrum $\mathit{ko}$ .

The map $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ was induced from a map of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces that factored through $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ , and therefore $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ factors through $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ . The homotopy groups of this spectrum are torsion, which follows from May’s definition [May77, §III.2] of $\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})$ and the triviality of the positive-degree rational stable homotopy groups of the sphere [Ser53]. Thus the rationalization $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})\wedge H\mathbb{Q}\simeq 0$ . For any class $x\in(\mathit{bo}_{0})^{0}(X)$ , if $J_{*}(x)$ has infinite order, its image in the rationalized $\mathit{bg\ell}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/\mathit{bstring}$ -cohomology of $X$ must be nonzero: because $X$ has finitely many cells in each dimension, its generalized cohomology groups for any finite-type spectrum (including all spectra appearing in this proof) are finitely generated, so infinite-order elements persist through rationalization. Rationally, though, $J_{*}$ passes through the zero spectrum. ∎

#### Remark 6.34.

One way to interpret this phenomenon is that, even though the first Pontrjagin class $p_{1}\colon B\mathrm{O}\to K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ descends to a map $p_{1}\colon B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}\to K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ , this map does not extend to a rationally nontrivial map out of $B\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathbb{S})/B\mathrm{String}$ . In the language of [DY23a], “a fake vector bundle with respect to twisted string structures has a first Pontrjagin class, but a fake spherical fibration does not.”

#### Remark 6.35 ( $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -families’ periodicity and Bernoulli numbers?).

Propositions 6.32 and 6.33 generalize mutatis mutandis to tangential structures further up the Whitehead tower of $B\mathrm{O}$ . To wit, given a natural number $n$ , let $\xi\colon B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}$ be the $(n-1)$ -connected covering map. This defines a tangential structure commonly called a $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structure, and the two-out-of-three data for $B\mathrm{O}$ pull back by the universal property of the $(n-1)$ -connected cover to define two-out-of-three data for $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures. (Compare Definition 6.28.) Thus Definition 6.1, Example 6.5, and Theorem 6.7 define vector bundle twists, non-vector-bundle twists, and Smith families for twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures just like for string structures.

For $n>4$ , the homotopy groups of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ are not all torsion, which is downstream from the isomorphism $\pi_{4}(B\mathrm{O})\cong\mathbb{Z}$ [Ste51, §24, §25]. Therefore, like for $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}$ , the order of a twist in $[X,B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle]$ is not a particularly good estimate for the value of the corresponding Smith family’s period. Indeed, Propositions 6.32 and 6.33 and their proofs generalize directly from $B\mathrm{String}$ to $B\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ , showing all Smith families of twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures have finite order, provided they are over spaces homotopy equivalent to CW complexes with finitely many cells in each dimension. One can also generalize this whole story to the limiting case as $n\to\infty$ , which is the tangential structure $E\mathrm{O}\to B\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. a stable framing.

Our proof did not give any estimates on the orders of these Smith families, just finiteness. It would be interesting to bound or compute these orders; for example, one could investigate the map of Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences induced by $j_{/\mathit{bo}\langle n\rangle}$ , the generalization of $j_{/\mathit{bstring}}$ in the proof of Proposition 6.32, or generalize Bauer’s proof in [Bau03, Lemma 2.1]. We suspect that sharp estimates for periodicity for Smith families of twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures will have formulas involving Bernoulli numbers, because of their appearance in Adams’ seminal work computing the image of the $J$ -homomorphism in $\pi_{*}(\mathbb{S})$ [Ada63, Ada65a, Ada65b, Ada66]. We would be interested in learning whether this is the case.

For $n\leq 16$ , twisted $\mathrm{O}\langle n\rangle$ -structures as defined here recover familiar twists of familiar tangential structures.

- (0) $\mathrm{O}\langle 0\rangle$ - and $\mathrm{O}\langle 1\rangle$ -structures are canonically equivalent to $\mathrm{O}$ -structures, i.e. no data, and so this story is vacuous.

- (2) $\mathrm{O}\langle 2\rangle$ -structures are equivalent to $\mathrm{SO}$ -structures, and this story recovers the twists in Example 6.19.

- (3) $\pi_{3}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ [Car36, §IV], and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 3\rangle$ and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 4\rangle$ are equivalent to $B\mathrm{Spin}$ . This story recovers the notion of twisted spin structure we discussed in Example 6.23.

- (5) $\pi_{k}(B\mathrm{O})$ vanishes for $k=5$ [Ste51, Remarks 24.11], $k=6$ [Eck51, 3.72], and $k=7$ [BS53, Proposition 19.5], so $B\mathrm{O}\langle 5\rangle$ , $B\mathrm{O}\langle 6\rangle$ , $B\mathrm{O}\langle 7\rangle$ , and $B\mathrm{O}\langle 8\rangle$ all coincide, and are $B\mathrm{String}$ . This story recovers the standard story of twists of string bordism that we mentioned in Example 6.17.

- (9) Sati-Schreiber-Stasheff [SSS09, Definition 1] call an $\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ -structure a fivebrane structure, and in a sequel paper [SSS12, §2.3], they introduce twisted fivebrane structures over a space $X$ given by data of a map $X\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ . It is possible to show that their definition is a special case of ours. Specifically, similarly to the identification $K(\mathbb{Z},4)\simeq B\mathrm{Spin}/B\mathrm{String}$ producing a map from the $K(\mathbb{Z},4)$ -twists of string bordism to the more general group of $B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{String}$ twists of string bordism [DY23a, (1.45)], the characteristic class $\tfrac{1}{6}p_{2}\colon B\mathrm{String}\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ induces an equivalence of grouplike $E_{\infty}$ -spaces $B\mathrm{String}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to K(\mathbb{Z},8)$ , and this equivalence leads to a map $K(\mathbb{Z},8)\simeq B\mathrm{String}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ carrying Sati-Schreiber-Stasheff’s twisted fivebrane structures to a subgroup of the fake vector bundle twists of fivebrane structure.

- (10) Sati [Sat15, Definition 2.4] calls $\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle$ -structures “ $2$ -orientations.” and studies their twists in (ibid., Definition 5.1). Like for twisted fivebrane structures, Sati’s twists are classified by maps to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,9)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ , and map to the twists we considered via the map $B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 9\rangle$ .

- (13) As $\pi_{11}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ [Bot59], $\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle$ - and $\mathrm{O}\langle 12\rangle$ -structures coincide. Sati refers to this as a “ $2$ -spin structure” [Sat15, Definition 2.5], and in (ibid., Definition 5.2) introduces twisted $2$ -spin structures corresponding to $K(\mathbb{Z}/2,10)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 10\rangle$ .

- (14) As $\pi_{k}(B\mathrm{O})=0$ for $k=13$ , $14$ , and $15$ [Bot59], $B\mathrm{O}\langle 13\rangle=\dotsb=B\mathrm{O}\langle 16\rangle$ . Sati [Sat15, Definition 3.1] names this tangential structure a ninebrane structure, and produces twisted ninebrane structures classified by the fractional Pontrjagin class $(1/240)p_{3}\colon B\mathrm{O}\langle 12\rangle\to K(\mathbb{Z},12)$ (ibid., Definition 5.3). As in the previous cases, the map $K(\mathbb{Z},12)\simeq B\mathrm{O}\langle 13\rangle/B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle\to B\mathrm{O}/B\mathrm{O}\langle 11\rangle$ sends Sati’s twists to ours.

Passing to the infinite limit, we obtain an interpretation of maps to $B\mathrm{O}/E\mathrm{O}$ , i.e. to $B\mathrm{O}$ , as classifying vector bundle twists of framed bordism. These twists of framed bordism are studied in [Cru03, FSS24].

## 7. Examples of Smith fiber sequences

In this section, we implement the discussion from the previous section for some commonly studied vector bundles. We find many previously studied Smith homomorphisms, and also identify a few other well-known cofiber sequences, including Wood’s sequences, Wall’s sequence, and the cofiber sequences associated to the Hopf maps and to transfer maps, as Smith homomorphisms (Examples 7.15 and 7.18). We include this Pokédex of examples in part to illustrate what kinds of Smith cofiber sequences are out there; in part to make contact with preexisting literature; and in part to illustrate how to put theorems such as Theorem 5.1 into practice to explicitly write down Smith cofiber sequences.

### 7.1. Twisting by real line bundles

Our first family of examples use the tautological line bundle $\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ ; its sphere bundle is the tautological $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle $E\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , whose total space is contractible. Therefore by Theorem 5.1, for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , we have a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k(\sigma-1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(k+1)(\sigma-1)}, $$

where $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ is the Smith homomorphism associated to $\sigma$ . When $k=0$ , this is especially nice: the middle spectrum is $\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\simeq\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and the map $\mathbb{S}\to\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is the inclusion of the first factor of the wedge sum, leading to a Smith isomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}\colon\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\overset{\simeq}{\to}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{\sigma}$ . This equivalence is well-known; see Kochman [Koc96, Lemma 2.6.5] for a proof.

#### Remark 7.2.

The Thom spectrum $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k\sigma}$ is often denoted in the homotopy theory literature by $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ , so that $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{k(\sigma-1)}$ can be identified with its desuspension $\Sigma^{-k}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ . One justification for this notation stems from (7.1): suspending it $k$ times gives a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}^{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}\longrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k+1}, $$

which exhibits $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k+1}$ as the spectrum obtained by crushing the bottom cell of $\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}_{k}$ .

#### Example 7.4.

Smash (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{O}$ . As every virtual bundle has a unique $MT\mathrm{O}$ -orientation, this cofiber sequence simplifies to

$$ MT\mathrm{O}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}MT\mathrm{O}\wedge\Sigma(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

This was the first Smith homomorphism studied; it was defined and named the Smith homomorphism by Conner-Floyd [CF64, Theorem 26.1]. Thom’s celebrated calculation of $\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{O}}$ [Tho54] implies that $MT\mathrm{O}$ is a sum of shifts of $H\mathbb{Z}/2$ ; on each of these copies, the Smith map (7.5) is the cap product with the nonzero element of $H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ .

Stong [Sto69, Proposition 5] and Uchida [Uch70] study related examples, where one smashes (7.5) with spaces $X$ ; they identify the fiber $MT\mathrm{O}\wedge X$ and show that the long exact sequence of homotopy groups splits. Their papers are among the earliest examples identifying the Smith long exact sequence.1616 16 At the time, it was common to think of $\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{O}}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)$ as the bordism groups of manifolds $M$ equipped with a free involution $\tau$ , rather than manifolds with a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle; Stong and Uchida’s results are phrased in that language. To pass between these perspectives, rewrite $(M,\tau)$ as the principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle $M\to M/\tau$ ; in the other direction, take the deck transformation involution of the total space of a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle.

#### Example 7.6.

Smash (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ . Since $\sigma$ is not orientable, but $2\sigma$ is oriented (see Example 6.12), we obtain a $2$ -periodic series of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms between the oriented bordism of $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted oriented bordism. The latter can be identified with unoriented bordism: a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted orientation on $V$ is data of a line bundle on $L$ and an orientation of $V\oplus L$ , which is no data at all: this identifies $L\cong\mathrm{Det}(V)^{\ast}\cong\mathrm{Det}(V)$ up to a contractible space of choices, and $V\oplus\mathrm{Det}(V)$ is canonically oriented. So every vector bundle has a canonical $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted orientation.

Therefore by Theorem 5.1 we obtain a $2$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms:

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{O} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

These maps are obtained by taking smooth representatives of Poincaré duals of $w_{1}$ either of the manifold (when the domain is $\Omega_{\ast}^{\mathrm{O}}$ ) or of the principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle (when the domain is $\Omega_{\ast}^{\mathrm{SO}}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)$ ). See [DDK+25, §IV.B] for the physical interpretation of the corresponding long exact sequence of Anderson dual groups.

These Smith homomorphisms were first introduced by Komiya [Kom72, §5]; see also Shibata [Shi73, Proposition 2.1]. See Córdova-Ohmori-Shao-Yan [COSY20, Appendix A], Hason-Komargodski-Thorngren [HKT20, §4.4], and Fidkowski-Haah-Hastings [FHH20] for applications of these Smith homomorphisms to physics. The splitting of the $k=0$ case of (7.1) implies a homotopy equivalence $MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\xrightarrow{\cong}\Sigma MT\mathrm{O}$ , a theorem of Atiyah [Ati61a, Proposition 4.1].

#### Example 7.8.

Some of the coolest examples of this kind come about by smashing (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ . As we discussed in Example 6.14, the periodicity of this family is $1$ , $2$ , or $4$ ; a Whitney sum formula calculation shows that $k\sigma$ is spin iff $k$ is a multiple of $4$ , and therefore this Smith family is $4$ -periodic. The corresponding $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted spin bordism groups can be identified with $H$ -bordism for certain Lie groups $H$ , as discussed in Example 6.23; specifically,

- (1) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to a pin $-$ structure;

- (2) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,2\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to an $H$ structure, where $H=\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ ; and

- (3) a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,3\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent to a pin $+$ structure.

Using Theorem 5.1 once again, the $4$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms takes the form

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4) \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}, $$

with each $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ obtained by taking a smooth representative of a Poincaré dual of $w_{1}$ of the manifold or of a associated principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle, like in (7.7).

The splitting of the $k=0$ Smith homomorphism in (7.1) gives us an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\simeq MT\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ , a theorem of Peterson [Pet68, §7].

This family of Smith homomorphisms has been discussed in the literature before. The piece involving $\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ was used by Peterson [Pet68, §7] and Anderson-Brown-Peterson [ABP69], who say that it was already “well-known.” The long exact sequence corresponding to (7.9c) appears in [Gia73b, Theorem 3.1], where it is attributed to Stong. The Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ in (7.9d) appears in Kreck [Kre84, §4]. The long exact sequence induced by (7.9b) is used by Botvinnik-Rosenberg [BR23, §2], who also discuss (7.9c) and (7.9d). The composition of two maps in (7.9) in a row to go between pin $+$ and pin $-$ bordism appears in Kirby-Taylor [KT90a, Lemma 7]. We work out the corresponding long exact sequences, as well as some physical consequences for all four Smith homomorphisms in [DDK+25, §IV.C].

The full family appears more recently in work of Hambleton-Su [HS13, §4.C], Kapustin-Thorngren-Turzillo-Wang [KTTW15, §8], Tachikawa-Yonekura [TY19, §3.1], Hason-Komargodski-Thorngren [HKT20, §4.4], and Wan-Wang-Zheng [WWZ20, §6.7]. Ekholm [Ekh98] produces the $4$ -periodic sequence of tangential structures in a different setting but does not discuss the Smith homomorphism.

#### Example 7.10.

As we discussed in Example 6.17, for a general vector bundle $V\to X$ , there is no guarantee that $kV$ has a string structure. However, on $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , $k\sigma$ has a string structure iff $k\equiv 0\bmod 8$ , so there is an eight-periodic family of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms between bordism groups of manifolds with $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted string structures for various $k$ .1717 17 To prove the claimed fact about string structures on $k\sigma$ , first use the Whitney sum formula to show that $w_{1}(k\sigma)$ , $w_{2}(k\sigma)$ , and $w_{4}(k\sigma)$ all vanish iff $k\equiv 0\bmod 8$ . The reduction mod $2$ map $H^{4}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})\to H^{4}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is an isomorphism, so the string obstruction $\lambda(k\sigma)$ vanishes iff its mod $2$ reduction does, and $\lambda\bmod 2=w_{4}$ .

In Example 7.8, each $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure for $k\in\mathbb{Z}/4$ turned out to be equivalent to a $G[k]$ -structure for four Lie groups $G[k]$ : $G[0]\cong\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ , $G[1]\cong\mathrm{Pin}^{-}$ , $G[2]\cong\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ , and $G[3]\cong\mathrm{Pin}^{+}$ (see also [TY19, (3.1)]). An analogous result is true for the eight twisted string structures, but in the world of $2$ -groups, because the string group is a Lie $2$ -group [SP11]. We will see that for each $k\in\mathbb{Z}/8$ , there is a Lie $2$ -group $\mathbb{G}[k]$ and a map $\xi\colon B\mathbb{G}[k]\to B\mathrm{O}$ such that $\mathbb{G}[k]$ -structures on a smooth manifolds are naturally equivalent to $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,k\sigma)$ -twisted string structures. Though it is difficult to describe $\mathbb{G}[k]$ explicitly for most $k$ , we will realize it as an extension of $G[k\bmod 4]$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ : such extensions of a compact Lie group $G$ by $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ are classified by $H^{4}(BG;\mathbb{Z})$ [SP11, Wei22], and we will find classes in this cohomology group classifying all eight $\mathbb{G}[k]$ $2$ -groups.

Recall from Example 6.23 that if $V\to X$ is a pin $\pm$ vector bundle, then $V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V)$ has a canonical spin structure, meaning that the string obstruction class $\lambda(V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V))\in H^{4}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is defined. Let

$$ \lambda^{\pm}\coloneqq\lambda(V\mp\mathrm{Det}(V))\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Pin}^{\pm};\mathbb{Z}). $$

The inclusion $j\colon\mathbb{Z}/2\hookrightarrow\mathrm{U}(1)$ pulls back the tautological complex line bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ to $2\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Therefore a $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,2\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure induces a $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin structure—or in the language of Example 6.23, a $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4$ structure induces a spin $c$ structure via $j$ . Let $\lambda^{c}\in H^{4}(B\mathrm{Spin}^{c};\mathbb{Z})$ be the class defined in [DY24a, Definition 2.6],1818 18 The class $\lambda^{c}$ is called $q_{2}$ in [Dua18] and $\widehat{p}_{2}$ in [CN19, §2.7]. In the notation of [CY20, (3.10)], $\lambda^{c}=c_{1}(L)^{2}-p_{c}$ , and in [Dev22, Construction 2], $\lambda^{c}=c_{1}(L)^{2}-(c_{1}^{2}-p_{1})/2$ , where $L$ is the determinant line bundle. namely $\lambda(V\oplus L)$ , where $L$ is the determinant bundle of the spin $c$ structure. Pulling back by $j$ , we will regard $\lambda^{c}$ as a class in $H^{4}(B(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/4);\mathbb{Z}/2)$ .

Thus, essentially by definition, for $k=-1,0,1,2\bmod 8$ , the obstruction to lifting from a $G[k\bmod 4]$ -structure to a $\mathbb{G}[k]$ -structure is respectively $\lambda^{+}(V)$ , $\lambda(V)$ , $\lambda^{-}(V)$ , and $\lambda^{c}(V)$ , where $V\to BG[k]$ is the tautological bundle. This gives the first half of Table 1.

Let $e^{\mathbb{Z}}\in H^{1}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z}_{w_{1}(\sigma)})$ denote the twisted $\mathbb{Z}$ -cohomology Euler class as defined in Definition 4.4 for $\mathcal{R}=H\mathbb{Z}$ . Čadek [Čad99, Lemma 1] shows that $(e^{\mathbb{Z}})^{2\ell}$ is an untwisted class, and moreover is the unique nonzero element of $H^{2\ell}(B\mathbb{Z}/2;\mathbb{Z})$ . Thus, since $4\sigma\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ is spin but not string (see Footnote 17), the class $\lambda(4\sigma)$ is defined and equals $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(\sigma)^{4}$ . The string obstruction $\lambda$ satisfies a Whitney sum formula [Deb24, Lemma 1.6] for pairs of spin vector bundles,1919 19 See also Johnson-Freyd and Treumann [JFT20, §1.4] for a proof sketch and Jenquin [Jen05, Corollary 4.9] for a similar result in a generalized cohomology theory. so for $k=3,4,5,6\bmod 8$ ,

#### Example 7.13.

If one smashes (7.1) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , one obtains a very similar story to Example 7.6: twice any vector bundle is complex, hence spin $c$ , and $(B\mathbb{Z}/2,\sigma)$ -twisted spin $c$ bordism is naturally identified with pin $c$ bordism, as we discussed in Example 6.21. So taking Poincaré duals of $w_{1}$ as in Example 7.6 defines a $2$ -periodic sequence of codimension- $1$ Smith homomorphisms

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

To our knowledge, these long exact sequences first appear in Hambleton-Su [HS13, §4.C].

We also obtain an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2\overset{\simeq}{\to}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Pin}^{c}$ , which was first observed by Bahri-Gilkey [BG87a, §3]. See Shiozaki-Shapourian-Ryu [SSR17, §E.1] and Kobayashi [Kob21, §IV] for applications in condensed-matter physics and [DYY25a] for an application of a closely related Smith long exact sequence.

#### Example 7.15.

Pull back (7.1) along the map $B\mathbb{Z}\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ , i.e. $S^{1}=\mathbb{RP}^{1}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$ . The sphere bundle of $\sigma\to\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ is not contractible: it is the double cover $S^{1}\to\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ , and its Thom space is $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ . Therefore we obtain from Theorem 5.1 a cofiber sequence $\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}S^{1}\to\Sigma^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\to\Sigma_{+}^{1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ , which is a rotated version of the multiplication-by- $2$ cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}. $$

The same story applies to the complex, quaternionic, and octonionic Hopf fibrations: their cofibers are the respective projective planes $\Sigma^{-2+\infty}\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ , $\Sigma^{-4+\infty}\mathbb{HP}^{2}$ , and $\Sigma^{-8+\infty}\mathbb{OP}^{2}$ , and in each case the map to the cofiber is a Smith homomorphism for the tautological line bundle over the respective projective line (which is a sphere). In the case of the complex Hopf fibration, after smashing with $\mathit{ko}$ or $\mathit{KO}$ , one obtains the Wood cofiber sequences [Woo63] $\Sigma\mathit{KO}\xrightarrow{\eta}\mathit{KO}\to\mathit{KU}$ and $\Sigma\mathit{ko}\xrightarrow{\eta}\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{ku}$ as rotated versions of Smith cofiber sequences.

Smash (7.16) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ and you obtain Wall’s cofiber sequence [Wal60, Theorem 3]

$$ MT\mathrm{SO}\overset{2}{\longrightarrow}MT\mathrm{SO}\longrightarrow\mathcal{W}, $$

where $\mathcal{W}$ is the Thom spectrum whose homotopy groups are the bordism groups of manifolds with an integral lift of $w_{1}$ . This follows from Atiyah’s identification of $\mathcal{W}\simeq\Sigma^{-1}MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ [Ati61a, §4], but it is also easy to directly check that an integral lift of $w_{1}$ is equivalent data to a $(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ -twisted orientation, using that $\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ is a $B\mathbb{Z}$ .

It is also interesting to smash (7.16) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ ; we work out the induced long exact sequence of bordism groups in low degrees in Figure 2, and this long exact sequence also appears in [DYY25a].

#### Example 7.18.

Let $\pi\colon E\to B$ be a principal $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -bundle and $L\coloneqq E\times_{\mathbb{Z}/2}\mathbb{R}\to B$ be the associated line bundle. Then we have a Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{L}\colon B^{-L}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B$ . The fiber is the Thom spectrum of the pullback of $L$ to its sphere bundle; the sphere bundle is $E$ and $\pi^{\ast}(L)$ is trivial, so Theorem 5.1 gives us a cofiber sequence

$$ B^{-L}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\overset{\tau}{\longrightarrow}\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}E. $$

#### Lemma 7.20.

The map $\tau$ in (7.19) is the Becker-Gottlieb transfer [Rou72, KP72, BG75] for $\pi$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to work universally with the Smith cofiber sequence $(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}B\mathbb{Z}/2\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}E\mathbb{Z}/2$ , i.e. $(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}\to\mathbb{S}$ , and to show that the latter map is the transfer for $E\mathbb{Z}/2\to B\mathbb{Z}/2$ .

This transfer map admits the following description: consider the map of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -spectra2020 20 This fact, and our argument using it, works for both Borel and genuine $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -spectra. $f\colon\mathbb{S}\to\Sigma^{1-\sigma}(\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}$ , whose cofiber is $\mathbb{S}^{-\sigma}$ . Upon taking homotopy orbits, we obtain a map $f_{h\mathbb{Z}/2}\colon\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}\to\mathbb{S}$ , and this is the transfer map.

If $G$ is a finite group and $V\in\mathit{RO}(G)$ , there is a natural equivalence of spectra $(\mathbb{S}^{V})_{hG}\simeq(BG)^{V}$ .2121 21 One quick way to prove this uses the Ando-Blumberg-Gepner-Hopkins-Rezk approach to Thom spectra [ABG+14a, ABG+14b]: both $(\mathbb{S}^{V})_{hG}$ and $(BG)^{V}$ are both the colimit of the $\mathrm{pt}/G$ -shaped diagram whose value on $\mathrm{pt}$ is $\mathbb{S}^{V}$ and whose value on the morphism set $G$ encodes the $G$ -action on $\mathbb{S}^{V}$ [ABG+14a, Theorem 1.17]. It is also possible to prove this more classically by working with Thom spaces. And taking homotopy orbits of $G$ -spectra preserves cofiber sequences, so the fiber of the transfer $f_{h\mathbb{Z}/2}$ is the map $(\mathbb{RP}^{\infty})^{-\sigma}\to\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{\infty}$ given by the “inclusion” of virtual representations $-\sigma\hookrightarrow 0$ , which is the Smith homomorphism we began with. ∎

In the case that $B$ is a finite CW complex, one can prove Lemma 7.20 more classically by adapting Cusick’s calculation [Cus85, Corollary 2.11] identifying the cofibers of transfer maps for double covers.

#### Remark 7.21.

For another example along the lines of (7.19), Morisugi [Mor09, Theorem 1.3] shows that the cofibers of certain Smith homomorphisms over compact Lie groups can be described as Becker-Schultz transfer maps [BS74, §4]. And Uchida [Uch69], motivated by the study of immersions, works out the Smith long exact sequences of a few special cases of Example 7.18, where $E=B\mathrm{O}(k)\times B\mathrm{O}(k)$ and $B=B(\mathrm{O}(1)\ltimes(\mathrm{O}(k)^{\times 2}))$ , where $\mathrm{O}(1)$ acts on $\mathrm{O}(k)^{\times 2}$ by swapping the two factors.

#### Remark 7.22.

The ease of modifying the Smith long exact sequence by a vector bundle twist suggests that Example 7.18 could be generalized to some sort of twisted transfer map. The relevant twisted transfer maps have been constructed by Kashiwabara-Zare [KZ18].

### 7.2. Twisting by complex line bundles

Now we consider the analogous family of examples arising from the tautological complex line bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ . Its sphere bundle is $E\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , which is contractible, so just like in (7.1), we have for any $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{k(L-2)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{(k+1)(L-2)}. $$

Again, when $k=0$ , this sequence splits, yielding another Smith isomorphism $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{U}(1)\xrightarrow{\cong}(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}$ . This equivalence is well-known, e.g. [Ada74, Example 2.1].

#### Example 7.24.

Let $G$ be one of $\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , or $\mathrm{U}$ ; then the tautological line bundle over $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ has a $G$ -structure, and $\mathit{MTG}$ is an $E_{\infty}$ -ring spectrum and we can make sense of $G$ -orientations. The $G$ -orientation on $L$ untwists the Thom spectrum, so smashing (7.23) with $\mathit{MTG}$ has a similar effect to Example 7.4: the result is a cofiber sequence

$$ \mathit{MTG}\longrightarrow\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}. $$

For $G=\mathrm{U}$ , this Smith homomorphism was first studied by Conner-Floyd [CF66b, §5], and also appears in Ray [Ray72, §3].

#### Lemma 7.26.

For $G=\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , or $\mathrm{U}$ , there is an $\mathit{MTG}$ -module equivalence

$$ \mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{k\geq 0}\Sigma^{2k}\mathit{MTG}. $$

#### Proof.

The zeroth step is splitting off the basepoint: $\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\simeq\mathit{MTG}\vee\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))$ . As noted above, $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{U}(1)\simeq(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}$ , and we have a Thom isomorphism $\mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))^{L}\simeq\mathit{MTG}\wedge\Sigma^{2}(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}$ of $\mathit{MTG}$ -modules. We are now in the same situation as at the beginning of the proof, but shifted up by $2$ , and we carry on in a similar way. ∎

#### Example 7.28.

Smash (7.23) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ ; the bundle $L\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ is oriented but not spin, so $2L$ is spin, and therefore we obtain a $2$ -periodic, codimension- $2$ family of Smith homomorphisms between the spin bordism of $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ and $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin bordism. A $(B\mathrm{U}(1),L)$ -twisted spin structure is equivalent data to a spin $c$ structure, as we discussed in Example 6.23, so this Smith family takes the form

$$ \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+} \displaystyle MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}. $$

The long exact sequence arising from (7.29a) was identified by Kirby-Taylor [KT90b, Corollary 6.12, Remark 6.14]. The splitting of (7.23) when $k=0$ leads to an equivalence $MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge B\mathrm{U}(1)\simeq\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , a theorem due to Stong [Sto68, Chapter XI]. We discuss the physical interpretation of (7.29) in [DDK+25, §IV.A].

It would be interesting to study analogues of this example for pin $c$ or pin $\tilde{c}\pm$ bordism and applications to invertible phases. Kirby-Taylor [KT90b, Remark 6.15] consider two additional analogues of (7.29a), one of which is related to a Smith long exact sequence for $G$ -bordism where $G\coloneqq\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathrm{O}(2)$ (see [DYY25b, §3.3]). Stehouwer [Ste22, §4] computes $G$ -bordism groups in low dimensions, and $G$ -bordism also appears in [DDHM22, DDHM24, DYY25a]. In addition, Hambleton-Kreck-Teichner [HKT94, §2] study a pin $-$ and pin $c$ analogue of Example 7.28.

As noted above, $S(L)$ is contractible as it is the total space of the universal fibration. Therefore, the other three corners of the square form a fiber sequence. To compute the fiber of $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , we notice that applying the classifying space functor to the short exact sequence $\mathbb{Z}/n\hookrightarrow\mathrm{U}(1)\xrightarrow{\times n}\mathrm{U}(1)$ gives a fibration $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ . Then, recognizing the map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as the classifying map for a principal $\mathrm{U}(1)$ -bundle over $\mathrm{U}(1)$ with total space $B\mathbb{Z}/n$ , we conclude that the fiber of the map $B\mathbb{Z}/n\to B\mathrm{U}(1)$ is exactly $\mathrm{U}(1)$ . So, $S(i^{*}L)\simeq S^{1}$ .

Next, we need to pull back $V_{1}$ along the projection $p\colon S(i^{*}L)\to B\mathbb{Z}/n$ . We have that $p^{*}(k(i^{*}L-1))\cong\bigoplus_{k}p^{*}(i^{*}L)$ . Since $L$ is oriented as a real vector bundle, its pullbacks are as well, so $p^{*}i^{*}L$ is oriented when considered as a real vector bundle over $S^{1}$ , and thus it is the trivial 2-plane bundle.

Therefore, we recognize the Thom spectrum $S(i^{*}L)^{kp^{*}(i^{*}L)}$ as

$$ \displaystyle S(i^{*}L)^{kp^{*}(i^{*}L)} \displaystyle\simeq(S^{1})^{k} \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}\textnormal{Th}(S^{1};0) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}(\Sigma_{+}^{\infty}S^{1}) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k}(\Sigma^{\infty}S^{1}\oplus\Sigma^{\infty}S^{0}) \displaystyle\simeq\Sigma^{2k+1}\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma^{2k}\mathbb{S}. $$

Thus for each $k\geq 0$ we have a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma^{2k+1}\mathbb{S}\vee\Sigma^{2k}\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{k\cdot i^{*}L}\longrightarrow B\mathbb{Z}/n^{(k+1)i^{*}L}. $$

Finally, we place $V_{1}$ in virtual dimension zero by taking $V_{1}=k(i^{*}L-2)$ , to be consistent with the other examples in this section, and obtain the cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma\mathbb{S}\vee\mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{k(i^{*}L-2)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{L}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathbb{Z}/n)^{(k+1)(i^{*}L-2)}. $$

#### Example 7.35.

Smash (7.34) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ . Like in Example 7.28, $i^{*}L$ is oriented but not spin, and $2i^{*}L$ is spin, so we obtain a $2$ -periodic, codimension- $2$ family of Smith homomorphisms between the spin bordism of $B\mathbb{Z}/n$ and $(B\mathbb{Z}/n,i^{*}L)$ -twisted spin bordism. Campbell [Cam17, §7.9] identifies the latter as bordism for the tangential structure $\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2n$ , explicitly giving us Smith cofiber sequences

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\vee MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{i^{*}L}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/k)_{+} \displaystyle\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\vee MT\mathrm{Spin}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/k)_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{i^{*}L}}\mathit{MT}(\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k). $$

$\mathrm{Spin}\times_{\{\pm 1\}}\mathbb{Z}/2k$ bordism appears in the mathematical physics literature in [Bel99, Bla00, BBC17, Cam17, GEM19, Hsi18, Jan18, Li19, GOP+20, DDHM22, Deb21, DL21, DDHM24, HTY22, DYY25a]; the case $k=2$ also appears in [Gia73a, TY19, FH20, HKT20, MV21]. The Smith homomorphisms in (7.36) for $n=4$ appear in [DDHM24]. We work out the Anderson-dualized long exact sequences corresponding to (7.36) for the $n=3$ case in [DDK+25, §IV.D], and for the $n=4$ case in [DDK+25, §IV.E].

#### Example 7.37.

We elaborate on Example 7.35 when $n=2$ . The rotation representation is isomorphic to $2\sigma$ , where $\sigma$ denotes the real sign representation; we will also let $\sigma$ denote the associated bundle over $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ .

Everything in Example 7.35 still works for $n=2$ , but now we have more options: we can start with an odd number of copies of $\sigma$ . In this case, the fiber of the Smith map is the Thom spectrum of the Möbius bundle $(\sigma-1)\to\mathrm{U}(1)$ ; one can directly check that the Thom space of $\sigma$ is $\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ , so the Thom spectrum of $\sigma-1$ is $\Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ . Therefore we have a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \Sigma^{-1+\infty}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\longrightarrow(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(2k-1)(\sigma-1)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}(B\mathbb{Z}/2)^{(2k+1)(\sigma-1)}. $$

Out of all the examples we have studied in this section, this is the first one where the pullback of $V$ to the sphere bundle of $W$ is nontrivial.

As usual, we smash (7.38) with various bordism spectra. The map $\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}$ is the composition of two iterations of $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ from (7.1), so some of the resulting cofiber sequences look familiar from that perspective. We only discuss a few examples, but plenty more are out there.

- • If we smash (7.38) with $MT\mathrm{SO}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence first discussed by Atiyah [Ati61a, (4.3)]: (7.39)

$$ \mathcal{W}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{O}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{O}, $$

where $\mathcal{W}$ is Wall’s bordism spectrum (see Example 7.15). Here we use the identifications $\Sigma MT\mathrm{O}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\mathcal{W}\simeq MT\mathrm{SO}\wedge\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{RP}^{2}$ , both due to Atiyah [Ati61a, §4], that we discussed in Examples 7.15 and 7.6, respectively.

- • If we instead smash (7.38) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence (7.40)

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb{RP}^{2}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Pin}^{\pm}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}}\Sigma^{2}MT\mathrm{Pin}^{\mp}, $$

In Figure 3, we calculate the long exact sequence on bordism groups corresponding to (7.40) (specifically, the pin $-$ to pin $+$ case) in low degrees. ### 7.3. A few more examples

In this section, we record some examples of Smith cofiber sequences that do not arise from real or complex line bundles.

#### Example 7.41.

Like our previous examples over $B\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ , we can study Smith homomorphisms for the tautological quaternionic line bundle $V\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . Once again, the sphere bundle of $V$ is contractible, as it is $E\mathrm{SU}(2)\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ , so we obtain Smith cofiber sequences like in (7.1) and (7.23):

$$ \mathbb{S}\longrightarrow(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{k(V-4)}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{4}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{(k+1)(V-4)}. $$

For $k=0$ , this sequence splits, yielding a third Smith isomorphism $\Sigma^{\infty}B\mathrm{SU}(2)\xrightarrow{\cong}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{V}$ . This equivalence is well-known, e.g. [Tam97, §2].

This bundle has a $G$ -structure for $G$ including $\mathrm{O}$ , $\mathrm{SO}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}$ , $\mathrm{Spin}^{c}$ , $\mathrm{U}$ , $\mathrm{SU}$ , and $\mathrm{Sp}$ , and in all of these cases, smashing with $\mathit{MTG}$ produces Smith homomorphisms similar to those in Examples 7.4 and 7.24. The proof of Lemma 7.26 still works in this setting, and for these $G$ we obtain $\mathit{MTG}$ -module splittings

$$ \mathit{MTG}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{k\geq 0}\Sigma^{4k}\mathit{MTG}. $$

When $G=\mathrm{Spin}$ , (7.43) is closely related to the splittings in Lemmas B.13 and B.15.

The Smith map (7.42), after smashing with $\mathit{MTSp}$ , was studied by Landweber [Lan68, §5] and Ray [Ray72, §3]. An analogue in self-conjugate bordism (see [SS68, §8]) was studied by Gozman [Goz77, §3].

#### Example 7.47.

Consider the Smith homomorphisms coming from the tautological rank- $3$ vector bundle $V\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ . The one-point compactification of $\mathfrak{so}(3)/\mathfrak{u}_{1}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{U}(1)\cong S^{2}$ . #### Example 7.51.

If we pull Example 7.47 back to $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ , we obtain a Smith long exact sequence which makes an appearance both in [DDK+25, §IV.F] and in Appendix B.

The tautological quaternionic line bundle over $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is not isomorphic to the bundle associated to $\mathfrak{su}_{2}\oplus\mathbb{R}$ , where $\mathfrak{su}_{2}$ is the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . Rather, since $\mathfrak{su}_{2}\cong\mathbb{R}\oplus\mathfrak{su}_{2}/\mathfrak{u}_{1}$ , the map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ exhibits $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as the unit sphere bundle in the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . It follows that there is a cofiber sequence

$$ B\mathrm{U}(1)\longrightarrow B\mathrm{SU}(2)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{V-3}, $$

where $V\to B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the vector bundle associated to $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ . We claim the first map is induced by the inclusion of a maximal torus into $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ . To see that the sphere bundle is $B\mathrm{U}(1)$ as claimed, identify $\mathrm{SU}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and $\mathrm{U}(1)\to\mathrm{SU}(2)$ with $\mathrm{Spin}(2)\to\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ ; by the third isomorphism theorem, $\mathrm{Spin}(3)/\mathrm{Spin}(2)\cong\mathrm{SO}(3)/\mathrm{SO}(2)$ , and in Example 7.47 we identified that quotient with the unit sphere inside $\mathbb{R}^{3}$ . Therefore taking associated bundles, we end up with $B\mathrm{Spin}(2)$ as the fiber in (7.52).

Since $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is simply connected, $B\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is $2$ -connected and therefore all of its vector bundles admit spin structures. Thus, when we smash (7.52) with $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ , we obtain a cofiber sequence

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\longrightarrow MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}\Sigma^{3}MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{SU}(2))_{+}. $$

The Thom spectrum $(B\mathrm{SU}(2))^{\mathfrak{su}(2)}$ is known as James’ “quasiprojective space” (see [Jam76]). The Anderson dual of (7.53) appears in a physics application in [DDK+25, §IV.F.].

The same Thom isomorphism applies for any $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ -oriented ring spectrum, such as $MT\mathrm{SO}$ or $\mathit{ko}$ ; if we used $\mathit{ko}$ instead of $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ in (7.53), we would obtain the cofiber sequence in (B.23).

#### Example 7.59.

The unit sphere bundle to the tautological bundle $V_{n+1}\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ is homotopy equivalent to the map $B\mathrm{O}(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n+1)$ . This is because $S^{n}\cong\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n)$ , so the unit sphere bundle can be described by the mixing construction

$$ S^{n}\times_{\mathrm{O}(n+1)}E\mathrm{O}(n+1)\cong(\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n))\times_{\mathrm{O}(n+1)}E\mathrm{O}(n+1)\cong E\mathrm{O}(n+1)/\mathrm{O}(n)\cong B\mathrm{O}(n). $$

## 8. Long exact sequence of invertible field theories

In this section, we turn to physical applications of the Smith fiber sequence (Theorem 5.1). In Section 8.1 we give a brief overview of anomalies and how they relate to invertible field theories. In Section 8.2 we review the mathematical classification of invertible field theories as Anderson dual groups of Thom spectra. In Section 8.3 we show how the Smith fiber sequence gives rise to a long exact sequence of invertible field theories (Corollary 8.20), which we call the symmetry breaking long exact sequence (SBLES). Finally, we give a mathematically-oriented introduction to our companion work [DDK+25] and a table of cross-listed examples (Table 2).

Quantum field theory is not yet completely mathematically formalized, and the applications of the Smith homomorphism in [HKT20, COSY20, DDK+25] take place at a physical level of rigor, not a mathematical one. As such, parts of this section are also only at a physical level of precision.

### 8.1. Anomalies and invertible field theories

Our homotopy-theoretic techniques in this paper apply to the classification of invertible field theories, while the physical objects we ultimately wish to study are (not necessarily invertible) quantum field theories with potentially anomalous symmetries. To apply our techniques, we take the following perspective on anomalies.2424 24 There are many things called “anomalies” in quantum field theory, and we are not claiming our definitions or approach is universal. Instead, our application is to a broad class of anomalies.

Let us first consider anomalies of symmetries. Physically, we begin with a $n$ -dimensional quantum system (such as a quantum field theory) with partition function $Z$ , as well as a symmetry group $G$ , which is usually a compact Lie group. We can couple the theory to a background $G$ -gauge field $A$ . Then, put simply, the $G$ symmetry is anomalous if the partition function evaluated on a pair of a closed $n$ -manifold $M$ and a background gauge field with connection $A$ is not gauge invariant but rather transforms with a phase. That is, under a gauge tranformation $A\mapsto A^{g}$ , the partition function transforms as

$$ Z(M,A^{g})=e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}Z(M,A), $$

where $e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}$ is a phase factor that cannot be cancelled by local counter-terms.

Mathematically, this means that when we evaluate the theory on a $n$ -dimensional manifold $M$ with a $G$ -principal bundle with connection $A$ , the partition function is a section of a non-trivial line bundle. The non-triviality of the line bundle is the anomaly.

To relate anomalies to invertible field theories, we use the notion of anomaly inflow: under mild hypotheses, and in all known cases, there is a local counterterm $e^{i\omega(K,A)}$ defined in one dimension higher, so that if $K$ is an $(n+1)$ -dimensional manifold with boundary and $\partial K=M$ (and $A$ extends into $K$ ), then

$$ e^{i\omega(K,A^{g})-i\omega(K,A)}=e^{i\alpha(M,A,g)}. $$

We may interpret $e^{i\omega(K,A)}$ as the partition function of an $n+1$ -dimensional invertible field theory with $G$ symmetry. It is invertible, as stacking with the $e^{-i\omega(K,A)}$ theory gives the trivial theory. Furthermore, $Z$ naturally lives at the boundary of this invertible theory, and together they are gauge invariant by Equation 8.2. Therefore we can interpret the existence of the $G$ -anomaly, which is the failure of $Z(M,A)$ to be gauge invariant, as the statement that $Z$ is a boundary theory of a non-trivial $(n+1)$ -dimensional invertible field theory, which we call the bulk theory. This perspective, formulated mathematically by Freed-Teleman [FT14], is the link between anomalies and invertible field theories; see also Freed [Fre23].

We also study anomalies of families of field theories parameterized by a topological space $X$ . An anomaly of an $X$ -family of field theories indicates a failure of the partition function to be consistently defined over the space of background $X$ -fields.2525 25 Typically in physics, $X$ carries more structures, such as a smooth structure or Riemannian metric. The anomalies we consider here will not depend on those structures. In this case, the bulk theory is an one-dimension-higher $X$ -family of invertible field theories. More generally, we can ask for $X$ to be a space with $G$ -action, and consider anomalies of $G$ -equivariant $X$ -families field theories. We refer the reader to [DDK+25, §II.A] and the references therein for more detail.

### 8.2. Invertible field theories and Thom spectra

Here we review the mathematical classification of (reflection-positive) invertible theories. First we must relate symmetries and tangential structures.

#### 8.2.1. Symmetries and tangential structures

For any tangential structure in the sense of Definition 2.3, there is a notion of topological field theory. Given a field theory whose anomaly we want to investigate, which tangential structure $\xi$ do we want our invertible field theories to carry?2626 26 For non-topological invertible field theories, there is also the question of enriching the tangential structure to something more geometric, such as including the data of a Riemannian metric or a connection for a principal bundle. At the level of invertible field theories this is accounted for by working with Anderson duals of bordism spectra, so our calculations include these geometric modifications.

The answer typically depends only on the symmetries of our field theory, not on its field content (the anomaly itself—which invertible field theory we get out of all the invertible field theories on $\xi$ -manifolds—uses more information from the theory). We follow Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §2], who take the stance that since we typically study QFTs in Minkowski signature but invertible field theories are Euclidean, we should Wick-rotate the group of symmetries to define our tangential structure.

Assume the dimension $n$ is at least $2$ . Let $\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ be the isometry group of Minkowski space, and let $\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}\subset\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ be the subgroup of isometries that preserve the direction of time. The group of symmetries of our theory is a Lie group $\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)$ with a map $\rho(n)\colon\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)\to\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}$ . Let $K\coloneqq\mathrm{ker}(\rho(n))$ ; we assume $K$ is compact. Assume that the normal subgroup of translations $\mathbb{R}^{1,n-1}\subset\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ lifts to a normal subgroup of $\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)$ , and let $H(1,n-1)\coloneqq\mathcal{H}(1,n-1)/\mathbb{R}^{1,n-1}$ . Now:

$$  $$

- (1) Let $\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}\coloneqq\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)\cap\mathcal{I}(1,n-1)$ . There is an exact sequence (8.3a)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow H(1,n-1)\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(1,n-1)^{\uparrow}. $$

- (2) This exact sequence can be extended to an exact sequence of complexifications: (8.3b)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K(\mathbb{C})\longrightarrow H(n,\mathbb{C})\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(n,\mathbb{C}), $$

- (3) and then to compact real forms of these complex Lie groups: (8.3c)

$$ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow H(n)\longrightarrow\mathrm{O}(n). $$

The tangential structure that the anomaly field theory has is $\xi\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ . Just as it is not a priori clear that the anomaly field theory extends to dimension $n+1$ , it is also not necessarily clear that $\xi$ extends to an $(n+1)$ -dimensional unstable tangential structure, but Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 2.19] prove that it does in nearly every situation one might want, as we discuss below. In this paper, we will always be in the situation that $\xi$ extends to $(n+1)$ -manifolds.

In practice, one can often use an idea of Stehouwer [Ste22] to compute $\xi$ using the formalism of fermionic groups (sometimes called supergroups).

#### Definition 8.4 (Benson [Ben88, §7]).

A fermionic group is a topological group $G$ together with data of:

- • a central element squaring to $1$ , which we call fermion parity and denote $-1\in G$ , and

- • a group homomorphism $\theta\colon G\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ such that $\theta(-1)=0$ .

We think of $\theta$ as defining a $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -grading on $G$ , and we refer to elements of $G$ as odd or even. The even elements form a subgroup $G_{0}\subset G$ , which is itself a fermionic group with $\theta$ trivial.

Given two fermionic groups $G$ and $H$ , one can take their fermionic tensor product (ibid.) $G\otimes H\coloneqq(G\times H)/\langle(-1,-1)\rangle$ . This is a fermionic group, with central element $(-1,1)=(1,-1)$ and grading $\theta((g,h))$ equal to the sum mod $2$ of the gradings on $g$ and on $h$ .

Fermionic groups describe symmetries of theories with fermions: $-1$ acts by fermion parity, which may mix nontrivially with other symmetries in the theory; and $\theta$ describes whether elements of $G$ act unitarily or antiunitarily. Given a fermionic group $G$ , Stolz [Sto98, §2.6] defines a tangential structure $\xi_{G}\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ as follows: let $H$ be the even subgroup of the fermionic tensor product $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\otimes G$ ; here, to make $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}$ into a fermionic group, we use the usual $-1$ , and the grading homomorphism is $\pi_{0}\colon\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\to\mathrm{O}(1)\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Then $B\coloneqq BH$ , and the map $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ is induced from the usual map $\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\to\mathrm{O}$ and the constant map to the identity on the quotient of $G_{0}$ by fermion parity. See [Ste22] for several examples of computations of tangential structures from data of the symmetries of a theory.

Tangential structures can encode not only the symmetries of quantum systems, but also the parameter space. For example, $S^{1}$ -families of fermionic theories with an internal unitary $\mathbb{Z}/2$ symmetry may be described using the tangential structure $B\mathrm{Spin}\times B\mathbb{Z}/2\times S^{1}\to B\mathrm{Spin}\to BO$ . There are also variations and twists: if $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $S^{1}$ , then we replace $B\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}\times S^{1}$ with the homotopy quotient $S^{1}/(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ . To encode a time-reversal symmetry $T$ with $T^{2}=(-1)^{F}$ , we replace $B\mathrm{Spin}\times B\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $B{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}$ . Note that the process of describing the symmetry and parameter space of a field theory can be subtle. See [DDK+25] for more examples of converting the data of symmetries and parameter spaces to tangential structures.

#### 8.2.2. Invertible field theories and bordism invariants

At this point in the story we have turned the physics question of determining the possible anomalies of a theory with a given collection of symmetries into the mathematical question of classifying (reflection-positive) invertible field theories for a fixed tangential structure $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ , with $B=BG$ .

In this subsubsection we discuss how this classification question reduces to a well-studied problem in algebraic topology: the computation of groups of bordism invariants. See Freed [Fre19, Lectures 6–9] and Galatius [Gal21] for more detailed reviews of this story.

Fix nonnegative integers $k\leq n$ ; $n$ will be the dimension of the field theories we consider and $k$ will be the category number. Let $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ denote the bordism $k$ -category of $\xi$ -manifolds, whose objects are closed $(n-k)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -manifolds, morphisms are ( $\xi$ -diffeomorphism classes rel boundary of) compact $(n-k+1)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -structured bordisms between them, $2$ -morphisms are ( $\xi$ -diffeomorphism classes rel boundary of) $(n-k+2)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -structured bordisms between bordisms, and so on; see [Lur09, CS19] for more details. We will also fix a symmetric monoidal (weak) $k$ -category $\mathsf{C}$ . The motivating cases, when $k=1$ , are the categories $\mathsf{Vect}$ and $\mathsf{sVect}$ of complex vector spaces, resp. super vector spaces, with tensor product as the symmetric monoidal structure.

Following Atiyah [Ati88] and Segal [Seg88], by a field theory we mean a symmetric monoidal functor $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ ; the dimension of this theory is $n$ .

#### Definition 8.5 (Freed-Moore [FM06, Definition 5.7]).

An $n$ -dimensional field theory $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ is invertible if there is some other theory $Z^{-1}$ such that $Z\otimes Z^{-1}$ is the trivial theory.

This tensor product is evaluated “pointwise,” meaning that $(Z\otimes Z^{-1})(M)\coloneqq Z(M)\otimes Z^{-1}(M)$ , where $M$ is an object, morphism, etc. in the bordism category; therefore invertibility implies that $Z$ , as a functor, factors through the Picard sub- $k$ -groupoid of units $\mathsf{C}^{\times}$ inside $\mathsf{C}$ , meaning that if $X$ is any object, morphism, or higher morphism in $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ , $Z(X)$ is invertible: $\otimes$ -invertible if $X$ is an object, and composition-invertible if $X$ is a (higher) morphism. If $X$ is invertible, then we must have data of an isomorphism $Z(X^{-1})\xrightarrow{\cong}Z(X)^{-1}$ because $Z$ is symmetric monoidal; thus, even if $X$ is not invertible, we can heuristically define $Z(X^{-1})\coloneqq Z(X)^{-1}$ as if $X^{-1}$ existed. These definitions are compatible as $X$ varies, in the sense that $Z$ extends to the Picard $k$ -groupoid completion $\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}$ of $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ : the Picard $k$ -groupoid defined by formally adding inverses to all objects, morphisms, higher morphisms, etc. of $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ . Thus, an invertible field theory $Z\colon\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}\to\mathsf{C}$ is equivalent data to a morphism of Picard $k$ -groupoids

$$ Z\colon\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}\longrightarrow\mathsf{C}^{\times}. $$

So to compute deformation classes of invertible field theories, we should compute the groups of symmetric monoidal functors between these Picard $k$ -groupoids, modulo natural isomorphisms. The homotopy theory of Picard groupoids embeds in the usual stable homotopy category: if $\mathsf{D}$ is a Picard groupoid, the geometric realization $\lvert N\mathsf{D}\rvert$ of the nerve of $\mathsf{D}$ has an $E_{\infty}$ -structure arising from the monoidal product on $\mathsf{D}$ , and the Picard condition implies $\lvert N\mathsf{D}\rvert$ is grouplike. Therefore it is equivalent data to a connective spectrum $\lvert\mathsf{D}\rvert$ , which we call the classifying spectrum of $\mathsf{D}$ . This turns out to be a complete invariant of Picard $k$ -groupoids.

#### Theorem 8.7 (Stable homotopy hypothesis (Moser-Ozornova-Paoli-Sarazola-Verdugo [MOP+22])).

There is an equivalence of $\infty$ -categories between the $\infty$ -category of Picard $k$ -groupoids and the $\infty$ -category of spectra whose homotopy groups vanish outside of $[0,k]$ .

#### Remark 8.8.

For $k=1$ , the stable homotopy hypothesis was originally a folklore theorem: proofs or sketches appear in [BCC93, HS05, Dri06, Pat12, JO12, GK14]. For $k=2$ , the stable homotopy hypothesis was proven by Gurski-Johnson-Osorno [GJO19].

Therefore we need to compute the group of homotopy classes of maps of spectra $\lvert\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}{}_{n}^{\xi}\rvert\to\lvert\mathsf{C}^{\times}\rvert$ . A reasonable first step would be to identify these two classifying spectra. For the domain, the Picard $k$ -groupoid completion of the bordism category, this is due to Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss [GMTW09] and Nguyen [Ngu17] for the bordism $(\infty,1)$ -category and to Schommer-Pries [SP24] for more general $(\infty,k)$ -categories.

#### Theorem 8.9 (Galatius-Madsen-Tillmann-Weiss [GMTW09], Nguyen [Ngu17], Schommer-Pries [SP24]).

If $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ denotes the $(\infty,k)$ -category of bordisms of $\xi_{n}$ -structured manifolds in dimensions $n-k,\dotsc,n$ , then there is a natural equivalence $\lvert\overline{\mathsf{Bord}}_{n}^{\xi}\rvert\simeq\Sigma^{k}\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ .

Here $\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ is a Madsen-Tillmann spectrum as in Definition 2.17.

Freed-Hopkins-Teleman [FHT10] then applied this result to classify invertible field theories in terms of $\mathit{MT\xi}_{n}$ . For that, one needs to determine $\lvert\mathsf{C}^{\times}\rvert$ , which of course depends on the choice of $\mathsf{C}$ —Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §5.3] argue that the (shifted) character dual of the sphere spectrum $\Sigma^{n}I_{\mathbb{C}^{\times}}$ is a universal choice, and that a related object called the (shifted) Anderson dual of the sphere spectrum $\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ should appear when one wants to classify deformation classes of invertible field theories. For applications to anomalies, we are interested in deformation classes, so use $\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ .

The Anderson dual $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ is characterized by its universal property that for any spectrum $\mathcal{X}$ , there is a short exact sequence [And69, Yos75]

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\pi_{n+1}\mathcal{X},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[\mathcal{X},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\pi_{n+2}\mathcal{X},\mathbb{Z})}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{0.}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi} $$

We are interested in anomalies of unitary QFTs, hence we expect the anomaly theories to satisfy the Wick-rotated analogue of unitarity: reflection positivity. Freed-Hopkins [FH21, §7.1, §8.1] define reflection positivity for invertible TFTs using $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -actions on $\mathsf{Bord}_{n}^{\xi}$ and $\mathsf{C}$ ,2727 27 The definition of reflection positivity for extended not-necessarily-invertible TFTs is still open: see [JF17, FHJF+24, Ste24, MS25] for work in this direction. and prove two key results allowing for a complete classification of reflection positive invertible TFTs following their definition.

#### Theorem 8.11 (Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 2.19]).

If $n\geq 3$ and $\xi_{n}\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ is a tangential structure arising from a representation $\rho\colon H(n)\to\mathrm{O}(n)$ with $H(n)$ a compact Lie group and $\mathrm{SO}(n)\subset\mathrm{Im}(\rho)$ , then there is a stable tangential structure $\xi\colon BH\to B\mathrm{O}$ such that $\xi_{n}$ is the pullback of $\xi$ along $B\mathrm{O}(n)\to B\mathrm{O}$ .

#### Theorem 8.12 (Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 5.23], Grady [Gra23]).

Suppose $\xi\colon BH(n)\to B\mathrm{O}(n)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 8.11. The abelian group of deformation classes of $n$ -dimensional, reflection positive invertible field theories on manifolds with $\xi$ -structure is naturally isomorphic to $[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+1}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ .

So after we require reflection positivity, the classification changes from unstable bordism to bordism in the usual sense, which is easier to calculate.

#### Remark 8.13.

There are some other approaches to the classification of invertible topological field theories, due to Yonekura [Yon19], Rovi-Schoenbauer [RS22], and Kreck-Stolz-Teichner (unpublished; see [Sto18]).

Theorem 8.12 has a nice interpretation from the point of view of anomalies. Using the defining property of $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ , there is a short exact sequence

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces 0} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Hom(\Omega_{n+2}^{\xi},\mathbb{Z})}} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{0,}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi} $$

where $\mathrm{Tors}(\text{--})$ denotes the torsion subgroup. Using the Pontrjagin-Thom theorem (Theorem 2.18) to interpret $\Omega_{k}^{\xi}$ geometrically as $\xi$ -manifolds modulo bordism, the first and third terms in this short exact sequence have anomaly-theoretic interpretations.

- • The quotient $\Hom(\Omega_{n+2}^{\xi},\mathbb{Z})$ is a free abelian group consisting of characteristic classes of $(n+2)$ -dimensional $\xi$ -manifolds; under this identification, the map $\psi$ sends an anomaly field theory to the corresponding anomaly polynomial, which is one degree higher, such as Chern-Simons and Chern-Weil forms. This data is visible to perturbative techniques, and is sometimes called the local anomaly.

- • The subgroup $\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))$ is identified with the torsion subgroup of $[\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}}]$ ; these are the reflection positive invertible field theories which are topological. Such field theories’ partition functions are bordism invariants, and the identification of these reflection positive invertible TFTs with $\mathrm{Tors}(\Hom(\Omega_{n+1}^{\xi},\mathbb{C}^{\times}))$ assigns to a reflection positive invertible TFT its partition function. Typically this data is invisible to perturbative methods and is called the global anomaly.

Yamashita-Yonekura [YY23] and Yamashita [Yam23] relate the short exact sequence (8.14) to a differential refinement of $\mathrm{Map}(\mathit{MT\xi},\Sigma^{n+2}I_{\mathbb{Z}})$ .

### 8.3. Long exact sequence of invertible field theories

Just as the map of spectra of Section 3.2 induces a Smith homomorphism on bordism, it dually induces a map of invertible field theories. Explicitly, we obtain this by mapping into the Anderson dual and taking homotopy groups. As in Section 3.1, consider a topological space $X$ , a tangential structure $\xi\colon B\to B\mathrm{O}$ , a virtual bundle $V\to X$ , and a vector bundle $W\to X$ of rank $r$ . As we discussed in the end of Section 8.2.1, the tangential structure encodes both symmetries of the theory as well as the parameter space.

#### Definition 8.15.

The defect anomaly map, generalized from [HKT20] section 4.2, is the map

$$ I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{W}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(X^{V}) $$

of invertible field theories induced by the zero section map.

Physically, we interpret $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(X^{V})$ to be classifying anomalies of QFTs in dimension $k-1$ with symmetry according to a $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure. The group mapping in, $I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})$ , classifies the anomalies of defect theories in dimension $k-r-1$ . These defect theories are created from the bulk theory, physically, by setting a non-trivial boundary condition on a symmetry-breaking order parameter, which corresponds to a section of the vector bundle $W$ . See [DDK+25, §III.A] for further explanation.

For clarity, we begin a running example.

#### Example 8.17.

Recall the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ family of examples from Example 7.8 and specifically Equation 7.9d:

$$ MT\mathrm{Pin}^{+}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}}\Sigma MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathbb{Z}/2)_{+}. $$

Here, we take $\xi$ according to spin bordism and twist with the tautological line bundle $W=\sigma$ over $X=B\mathbb{Z}/2$ . We take $V=3\sigma$ and apply the results of Section 6 to simplify (i.e., we use the fact that $4\sigma$ is spin). The corresponding map on invertible field theories is

$$ I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega_{\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2}^{k-1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{\sigma}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega_{{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}}^{k}. $$

Physically, we begin with a field theory with a pin+ symmetry; that is, a fermionic theory with an additional time reversal symmetry $T$ that squares to fermion parity: $T^{2}=(-1)^{F}$ . We require the physical assumption that there is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -odd bosonic operator $\phi$ such that the theory is gapped when the theory is deformed by $\phi$ . One example is the Majorana mass term for $2+1$ D Majorana fermions (see [DDK+25, §III.A.1]). We can define the theory on any manifold $M$ with a pin+ structure $P\colon M\to B{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}$ on its tangent bundle. If we choose generic configuration for the $\phi$ field, i.e., choose a section of the tautological line bundle $P^{*}\sigma$ , we arrive at an effective theory whose excitations are localized at the zero set of $\phi$ . We view this as a theory in one dimension lower, which is called a domain wall theory. Note that the bordism class of the zero set of $\phi$ is precisely the image of $[M]$ under $\mathrm{sm}_{\sigma}$ in (8.18). The domain wall theory no longer has the symmetry of the bulk theory: instead, it is a fermionic theory with a unitary internal symmetry $U$ squaring to $1$ ; i.e. it has $\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2$ tangential structure. We direct the reader to [DDK+25, §III.A] and [HKT20, §3.1] for more details.

In this context, anomaly matching refers to the process of identifying pairs of preimages and images of anomaly classes under the defect anomaly map $\mathrm{Def}_{W}$ . To perform anomaly matching, we must understand not only the two groups classifying the possible bulk and defect theories, but also the kernel and cokernel of the map $\mathrm{Def}_{W}$ . In some cases, one may deduce that information from an understanding of explicit bordism generators, but in general this approach is difficult. To address this question, we derived the map of spectra and identified its fiber, forming the Smith fiber sequence of Section 5. Now, just as for bordism, we may form a long exact sequence.

#### Corollary 8.20.

Applying $I_{\mathbb{Z}}$ to the cofiber sequence (5.3), we obtain the following long exact sequence of Anderson-dualized bordism groups, or in light of Theorem 8.12, groups of invertible field theories:

$$ \dotsb\longrightarrow I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{W}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(X^{V})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Res}_{W}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k}_{\xi}(S_{X}(W)^{V})\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Ind}_{W}}I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{k-r+1}_{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})\longrightarrow\dotsb $$

This long exact sequence is our mathematical model for the symmetry-breaking long exact sequence (SBLES) of [DDK+25] (see Table 2). In addition to the defect anomaly map $\mathrm{Def}_{W}$ defined in Definition 8.15, we call $\mathrm{Res}_{W}$ the residual anomaly map and $\mathrm{Ind}_{W}$ the index anomaly map.

#### Example 8.22.

In degree $k=4$ , there is a map of invertible field theories

$$ I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{3}_{\mathrm{Spin}\times\mathbb{Z}/2}\cong\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/8\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Def}_{\sigma}}\mathbb{Z}/16\cong I_{\mathbb{Z}}\Omega^{4}_{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}. $$

The $\mathbb{Z}/16$ classifies anomalies of Majorana fermions in $2+1$ dimensions. An associated domain wall theory often has $1+1$ d chiral fermion modes. To answer the question of what particular chiral fermions can live on the domain wall, we need to identify the map $\mathrm{Def}_{\sigma}$ in (8.23). To do so, we turn to the long exact sequence of invertible field theories, which we draw out in Figure 1.

By exactness, we deduce that the defect matching map in degree $k=4$ sends $(a,b)\in\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/8$ to $-a+2b\in\mathbb{Z}/16$ . This matches with the physical computation in [HKT20, §3.1], and its physical significance is discussed further there and in [DDK+25, §III.C.3].

As a computational tool, the long exact sequence allows us to determine the defect matching maps with ease. Moreover, the other two maps in the SBLES (8.21) also have physical interpretations. The residual anomaly map classifies the obstruction to gapping a QFT after symmetry breaking, as we explain in [DDK+25, §III.B], while the index anomaly map generalizes the relationship between Berry phases and the ground-state degeneracy in $0+1$ D systems; see [DDK+25, §III.C].

## Appendix A The Long Exact Sequence in Bordism

In this appendix, we explicitly describe the Smith long exact sequence of bordism groups and work through an example. As in Section 5, let $(X,\xi)$ be a stable tangential structure, let $V$ be a virtual bundle over $X$ , and let $W$ be a real vector bundle over $X$ of rank $r$ . The corresponding long exact sequence of bordism groups of Corollary 8.20 is

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dots\to\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(X^{V})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k-r}(X^{V+W-r})} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Omega^{\xi}_{k-1}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})\to\cdots} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{sm}_{W}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\delta} $$

Here, $p\colon S_{X}(W)\to X$ is the projection, $\mathrm{sm}_{W}$ is the Smith homomorphism, and $\delta$ is the connecting map. In this section, we will be explicit about taking the pullback $p^{*}V$ of $V$ to $S_{X}(W)$ .

Starting from the left, $\Omega_{k}^{\xi}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})$ is the bordism group of $k$ -manifolds $M$ equipped with a map $f\colon M\to S_{X}(W)$ together with a $\xi$ -structure on $TM\oplus f^{*}(p^{*}V)$ . Next, $\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(X^{V})$ is the bordism group of $k$ -manifolds equipped with a map to $X$ with the analogous twisted $\xi$ -structure, and $\Omega_{k-r}^{\xi}(X^{V+W-r})$ is the bordism group of $(k-r)$ -manifolds $N$ equipped with a map $g$ to $X$ with a $\xi$ -structure on $TM\oplus g^{*}V\oplus g^{*}W$ . Note that the Smith homomorphism lowers the dimension by $r$ and twists the tangential structure condition by $W$ .

Now we describe each map at the level of manifolds.

- (1) $p$ : Let $M$ be a closed $k$ -manifold equipped with a map $h\colon M\to S_{X}(W)$ such that $TM\oplus h^{*}V$ has a $\xi$ -structure, so that $M$ represents a bordism class in $\Omega^{\xi}_{k}(S_{X}(W)^{p^{*}V})$ . The image of $M$ under $p$ is represented by the same manifold $M$ with an $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure given by the composition with the projection. That is, equip $M$ with the map $M\overset{h}{\longrightarrow}S_{X}(W)\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}X$ .

- (2) $\mathrm{sm}_{W}$ : Now let $M$ be a closed $k$ -manifold equipped with a map $f\colon M\to X$ such that $TM\oplus f^{*}V$ has a $\xi$ -structure. Let $s\colon M\to W$ be a generic section, which is transverse to the zero section $s_{0}$ . Then, the intersection $N\coloneqq s(M)\pitchfork s_{0}(M)$ is a $(k-r)$ -dimensional manifold. Let $g$ be the composite $g\colon N\hookrightarrow M\overset{f}{\to}X$ . Since the normal bundle $\nu$ to $N$ satisfies $\nu\cong f^{*}W|_{N}=g^{*}W$ , $TM|_{N}\cong TN\oplus\nu\cong TN\oplus g^{*}W$ , and hence $N$ carries an $(X,V+W)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure coming from the $(X,V)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure on $M$ . We have $\mathrm{sm}_{W}\colon M\mapsto N$ .

- (3) $\delta$ : This is the connecting map in the long exact sequence. Start with a closed $k-r$ -manifold $N$ with an $(X,V+W)$ -twisted $\xi$ -structure given by, as above, $g\colon N\to X$ and a $\xi$ -structure on $TN\oplus g^{*}V\oplus g^{*}W$ . We claim that $S_{N}(g^{*}W)$ is the image under $\delta$ of $N$ , but it remains to show that $S_{N}(g^{*}W)$ has the appropriate tangential structure. This will be a corollary of a general splitting result of tangent bundles of sphere bundles. Lemma A.2. For any vector bundle $\pi\colon V\to B$ , there is an isomorphism of vector bundles, canonical up to a contractible space of choices, (A.3)

$$ TS(V)\oplus\underline{\mathbb{R}}\xrightarrow{\cong}\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus\pi^{*}(V). $$

Combining this with the previous paragraph, (A.4)

$$ TS(V)\oplus\nu\cong\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus T_{v}S(V)\oplus\nu\cong\pi^{*}(TB)\oplus\pi^{*}(V), $$

Let us now go through the long exact sequence of bordism groups for the Smith map 7.40. In this case, the Smith homomorphism is a map

$$ \mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}\colon\Omega_{k}^{{\mathrm{Pin}^{-}}}\longrightarrow\Omega_{k-2}^{{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}} $$

between the bordism group of $k$ -dimensional pin $-$ manifolds to the bordism group of $(k-2)$ -dimensional pin $+$ manifolds, described by sending a pin $-$ manifold $M$ to any closed submanifold $N$ whose homology class is Poincaré dual to $w_{1}(M)^{2}$ . #### Definition A.6.

Define a map $p\colon\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)\to\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{Pin}^{-}}$ by sending $(N,f\colon N\to\mathbb{RP}^{1})$ to $N$ .

#### Lemma A.7.

If $N$ has an $(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure, then $N$ has a canonical pin $-$ structure (so the map $p$ lands in pin $-$ bordism as claimed).

#### Proof.

The orientation of $TN\oplus f^{*}\sigma$ is equivalent data to an isomorphism $\mathrm{Det}(TN)\xrightarrow{\cong}f^{*}\sigma$ , so we obtain a spin structure on $TN\oplus\mathrm{Det}(TN)$ , i.e. a pin $-$ structure. ∎

The third map in the long exact sequence is the connecting map $\delta\colon\Omega_{*}^{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}\to\Omega_{*+1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ . The map $\delta$ sends a pin $+$ manifold $M$ to the total space of the sphere bundle $S(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))$ .2828 28 Note that $S(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))\simeq S(g^{*}(2\sigma))$ . The key to understanding $\delta$ is showing that $S(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))$ has a $(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ -twisted spin structure; in particular, we must cook up a map to $\mathbb{RP}^{1}$ .

#### Definition A.8.

Given a pin $+$ manifold $M$ , choose a metric on $\mathrm{Det}(TM)$ (a contractible choice); then, given $x\in M$ and $p,q\in\sigma_{x}$ with $\sqrt{\lvert p^{2}\rvert+\lvert q^{2}\rvert}=1$ , so that $(x,p,q)\in S(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))$ , the two sections of $\pi^{*}(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))$

$$ \displaystyle(x,p,q) \displaystyle\mapsto(p,q) \displaystyle(x,p,q) \displaystyle\mapsto(-q,p) $$

are everywhere linearly independent, so $\pi^{*}(2\mathrm{Det}(TM))$ is canonically trivial. #### Definition A.10.

The maps $\mathrm{sm}_{2\sigma}$ , $p$ , and $\delta$ assemble into a long exact sequence in bordism, as we will draw in Figure 3. To write out this long exact sequence, we need to know the relevant bordism groups in low dimensions. Giambalvo [Gia73b, §2, §3] computes $\Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Pin}^{+}}$ for $k\leq 12$ , more than good enough for us, and gives generating manifolds in all degrees we need except $k=2,3$ (though see [KT90a] for a correction); the rest were given by Kirby-Taylor [KT90b, Proposition 3.9, Theorem 5.1]. #### Lemma A.13.

There is an abelian group $A$ of order $4$ such that

$$ \Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)\cong\begin{cases}\mathbb{Z}/2,&k=0,1,3,4\\
A,&k=2\\
0,&k=5.\end{cases} $$

We may start the computation of $\Omega^{\mathrm{Spin}}(\mathbb{RP}^{1},\sigma)$ using the observation of Kirby and Taylor [KT90b] that the degree two map
