## Appendix B Computation of a Cobordism Euler Class

To compute the Smith homomorphism, it often suffices to take a Poincaré dual of the $\mathbb{Z}$ - or $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -cohomology Euler class of a vector bundle $V\to X$ , for example in [KTTW15, COSY20, HKT20]. However, our general definition (Definition 4.27) of the Smith homomorphism instead uses the (possibly twisted) $\xi$ -cobordism Euler class, tying more closely with invertible field theories. In this appendix, we walk through a concrete, low-dimensional example of a cobordism Euler class that goes beyond the cohomological approximation.

Recall that a spinh structure is a $(B\mathrm{SO}(3),V_{3})$ -twisted spin structure, where $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is the tautological vector bundle. Then, as we discussed in (7.49a), there is a Smith homomorphism

$$ \mathrm{sm}_{V}\colon\Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\to\Omega_{k-3}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3)). $$

#### Theorem B.2.

Give $S^{4}$ the spinh structure whose $\mathrm{SO}_{3}$ -bundle is classified by either map $S^{4}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ whose homotopy class generates $\pi_{4}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\cong\mathbb{Z}$ .

- (1) Exactness of the Smith long exact sequence forces $\mathrm{sm}_{V}(S^{4})$ to be the bordism class of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ with constant map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ in $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ .

- (2) $e(V)\in H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z})=0$ , and there is no way to assign every smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e(V)$ a spin structure whose bordism class equals that of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ .

- (3) The spin cobordism Euler class of $V$ is nonzero, and all smooth representatives of its Poincaré dual have the spin bordism class of $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ and a constant map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ .

This is why the cohomology Euler class does not suffice in this example.

We work with $\xi=\mathrm{Spin}$ and its twists throughout this appendix; see Remark B.36 for other tangential structures. Let $\mathit{ko}$ denote the connective real $K$ -theory spectrum; work of Anderson-Brown-Peterson [ABP67] shows that the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map $MT\mathrm{Spin}\to\mathit{ko}$ [ABS64] is $7$ -connected, meaning that as long as we restrict to manifolds of dimension $7$ and below, we may replace twisted spin bordism with twisted $\mathit{ko}$ -homology; in particular, we will work with $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology Euler classes.

Another consequence of the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map is that vector bundles with spin structure are oriented for $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology, meaning that if $V\to X$ is a spin vector bundle, the Euler class $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)$ that a priori lives in $\mathit{ko}^{r}(X^{V-r})$ in fact can be passed by the Thom isomorphism to $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)\in\mathit{ko}^{r}(X)$ .

We will compute these Euler classes by using a formula for the Thom class in equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory. Recall that the Clifford algebra $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded $\mathbb{R}$ -algebra on $n$ odd generators $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n}$ that anticommute and each square to $1$ ; likewise $\mathit{C\ell}_{-n}$ is the free $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded $\mathbb{R}$ -algebra on $n$ anticommuting odd elements $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n}$ , each squaring to $-1$ . See Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64] for more on Clifford algebras.

When discussing modules, tensor products, Morita equivalence, etc. for Clifford algebras, we will always consider the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -grading and take the Koszul sign rule into account. We will use $\hat{\otimes}$ to denote this $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded tensor product.

Let $G$ be a compact Lie group and $(X,A)$ a pair of $G$ -spaces such that $X/A$ is compact. Then, following Karoubi [Kar68, Kar02], we will represent classes in $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(X)$ as (equivalence classes of) $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module bundles over $X$ equipped with a $G$ -invariant trivialization over $A$ .

#### Theorem B.3 (Atiyah [Ati68, Theorem 6.1]).

Let $G$ be a compact Lie group, $X$ be a compact $G$ -space, and $V\to X$ be an $8k$ -dimensional spin $G$ -equivariant vector bundle. Let $\mathcal{S}\to X$ denote the associated spinor bundle. Let $u\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{0}(V,V\setminus 0)$ be the class obtained from the $G$ -equivariant Clifford module bundle associated to $\mathcal{S}$ by the method of Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64, §11]. Then the $G$ -equivariant Thom class of $V$ is $U_{G,V}\coloneqq w^{-k}u\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{8k}(V,V\setminus 0)$ , where $w\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{-8}(\mathrm{pt})$ is the Bott class.

Recall the exceptional isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ , and recall that $\mathit{ko}^{*}\cong\mathbb{Z}[\eta,v,w]/(2\eta,\eta^{3},2v,4w-v^{2})$ with $\lvert\eta\rvert=-1$ , $\lvert v\rvert=-4$ , and $\lvert w\rvert=-8$ .3232 32 The negative grading is a feature of generalized cohomology: for any spectrum $E$ , $E^{k}(\mathrm{pt})=E_{-k}(\mathrm{pt})=\pi_{-k}(E)$ .

The following result is stated without proof by Davis-Mahowald [DM79, §2]; see Bruner-Greenlees [BG10, Theorem 5.3.1] for a proof.

#### Proposition B.4.

There is an isomorphism of $\mathit{ko}^{*}$ -modules $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ with $\lvert p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=4$ .

The class $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ is called the first symplectic $\mathit{ko}$ -Pontrjagin class. The specific isomorphism in Proposition B.4 can be fixed uniquely by requiring that the image of $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ under $\mathit{ko}\to H\mathbb{Z}$ is the usual first symplectic Pontrjagin class, which is positive on the tautological quaternionic line bundle over $\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ .

Given a rank- $3$ spin vector bundle $V\to X$ , let $\mathcal{S}_{V}\to X$ be the associated spinor bundle, which is the quaternionic line bundle associated to the accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . We will show how the following result is a corollary of Theorem B.3.

#### Corollary B.5.

Let $V\to X$ be a rank- $3$ vector bundle with spin structure. Then $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(V)\in H^{3}(X;\mathbb{Z})$ and $e^{\mathbb{Z}/2}(V)\in H^{3}(X;\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish, and

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)=\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{V})\in\mathit{ko}^{3}(X). $$

We thank an anonymous referee for help with the following proof.

#### Proof sketch of Corollary B.5.

We first make two reductions.

- (1) The connective covering map $\mathit{ko}^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2})\to\mathit{KO}^{3}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2})$ is an isomorphism: since $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ is $2$ -connected, all maps $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}\to\Sigma^{3}\mathit{KO}$ factor through the $2$ -connected cover of $\Sigma^{3}\mathit{KO}$ , which is $\Sigma^{3}\mathit{ko}$ . The connective cover map $\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{KO}$ sends Euler classes to Euler classes; therefore it suffices to show $e^{\mathit{KO}}(V)=\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ (where here we abuse notation and let $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ denote its image in $\mathit{KO}$ -cohomology).

- (2) We can reduce further to a question in the $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory of a point. Specifically, the Atiyah-Segal completion theorem [AS69, Corollary 2.2] (see also [AH61]) identifies the “Borelification” map (B.7)

$$ \mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{*}(\mathrm{pt})\longrightarrow\mathit{KO}^{*}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2}) $$

as completion at a certain ideal, so if we can produce preimages of $e^{\mathit{KO}}(V)$ and $\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ under (B.7), then show that they are equal, this will suffice to finish the proof.

Given a compact Lie group $G$ and a $d$ -dimensonal real spin $G$ -representation $W$ , let $e_{G}^{\mathit{KO}}(W)\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{d}(\mathrm{pt})$ denote the $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -Euler class, defined to be the pullback of the equivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory Thom class $U_{G,W}\in\mathit{KO}_{G}^{d}(W,W\setminus 0)$ under the zero section. Atiyah [Ati68, §6] shows that the Atiyah-Segal completion map sends $U_{G,W}$ to the nonequivariant $\mathit{KO}$ -theory Thom class of the associated bundle $W\to BG$ ,3333 33 We thank Yigal Kamel for help with this point. so the analogous fact is true for Euler classes: the image of $e_{G}^{\mathit{KO}}(W)$ under (B.7) is $e^{\mathit{KO}}(W)\in\mathit{KO}^{d}(BG)$ .

Let $\mathbf{2}$ denote the defining representation of $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ and $[\mathbf{2}]$ denote its class in $\mathit{RSp}(\mathrm{SU}_{2})\cong\mathit{KSp}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{0}(\mathrm{pt})\cong\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{4}(\mathrm{pt})$ .3434 34 The notation $\mathbf{2}$ means that this representation is two-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$ ; we work over $\mathbb{R}$ , so think of $\mathbf{2}$ as four-dimensional. Bruner-Greenlees [BG10, Theorems 5.3.1 and 5.3.5] show that $2-[\mathbf{2}]$ is a preimage of $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S})$ under the completion map. To summarize, it now suffices to show that $e_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{\mathit{KO}}(V)=\eta(2-[\mathbf{2}])$ in $\mathit{KO}^{3}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}(\mathrm{pt})$ .

To proceed, we reduce this to a purely algebraic question. As mentioned above, we may represent elements of $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(\mathrm{pt})$ as equivalence classes of finite-dimensional real vector spaces with commuting $G$ -representation and $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module structures, and we may represent elements of $\mathit{KO}_{G}^{n}(W,W\setminus 0)$ as $G$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{n}$ -module bundles over $W$ , equipped with $G$ -invariant trivializations on $W\setminus 0$ . Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro [ABS64, §5] show that $\eta\in\mathit{KO}^{-1}(\mathrm{pt})$ is represented by $\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ as a module over itself; giving this module the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action produces a representative of $\eta\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{-1}(\mathrm{pt})$ . Thus, $\boldsymbol{2}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ (with $\boldsymbol{2}$ regarded as purely even) is a $\mathit{C\ell}_{4}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}$ -module. For $1\leq m\leq n$ , there is a Morita equivalence

$$ \mathsf{Mod}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}}\overset{\simeq}{\longrightarrow}\mathsf{Mod}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}} (\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m},\mathit{C\ell}_{n-1}) M(n,m)\coloneqq\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\underbracket{\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\dotsm\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}}_{\text{$m$ copies}}, $$

with bimodule data given by:

- • $e_{1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1,\dotsc,e_{n-m}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1\in\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}$ act by left multiplication by $e_{1},\dotsc,e_{n-m}$ on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-m}$ , tensored with the identity on the $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ factors.

- • $e_{n-m+i}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}1\in\mathit{C\ell}_{n}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-m}$ acts on the left by the identity on $\mathit{C\ell}_{n-1}$ tensored with $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ factor of $\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1}$ , and the identity on the remaining factors.

This Morita equivalence follows from the standard isomorphism of $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -graded algebras $\mathit{C\ell}_{1}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}\cong\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{R}^{1\mid 1})$ (see, for example, [DG18, Lemma 6.17]).

Specializing to $n=4$ and $m=1$ , and giving this bimodule the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action, we see that the class $[\boldsymbol{2}]\eta\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(\mathrm{pt})$ is represented by the $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -module

$$ (\boldsymbol{2}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathbb{R}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1})\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{4}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-1}}M(4,1). $$

For the Euler class, we use Atiyah’s Theorem B.3 identifying the $G$ -equivariant Thom class of an $8k$ -dimensional spin vector bundle. Apply this to $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ , an $8$ -dimensional $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -representation, thought of as an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant vector bundle over $\mathrm{pt}$ . Since $B\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ is $3$ -connected, all $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -representations $\rho$ are spin, as $w_{2}(\rho)\in H^{2}(B\mathrm{SU}_{2};\mathbb{Z}/2)=0$ . Therefore we learn from Theorem B.3 that the Thom class $U\coloneqq U_{\mathrm{SU}_{2},V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}}$ of $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ is, as an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{8}$ -bundle, constructed by Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro’s method [ABS64, §11] from the spinor representation $\mathcal{S}$ of $\mathrm{Spin}_{8}$ restricted by the standard inclusion $\mathrm{SU}_{2}\cong\mathrm{Spin}_{3}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Spin}_{8}$ . Thus we have an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{8}$ -module bundle

$$ U\in\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{8}(V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5},(V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5})\setminus 0)\cong\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{8}(\Sigma^{5}(V,V\setminus 0)). $$

The suspension isomorphism identifies this group with $\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(V,V\setminus 0)$ ; to see this in terms of Clifford modules, use the trivial $\mathbb{R}^{5}$ summand of $V\oplus\mathbb{R}^{5}$ to define a $\mathit{C\ell}_{-5}$ -action on $U$ in a similar manner to [BE23, §4.1]. The fiber $U_{0}$ over $0\in V$ is therefore a $(\mathit{C\ell}_{8}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-5})$ -module with commuting $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action. Now use the Morita equivalence (B.8a) with $n=8$ and $m=5$ , and give the bimodule $M(8,5)$ implementing this Morita equivalence the trivial $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -action. Then $U_{0}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}_{\mathit{C\ell}_{8}\mathbin{\hat{\otimes}}\mathit{C\ell}_{-5}}M(8,5)$ is an $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -module, hence defines a class in $\mathit{KO}_{\mathrm{SU}_{2}}^{3}(\mathrm{pt})$ .

What remains is a tedious but straightforward computation to identify the classes of these two $\mathrm{SU}_{2}$ -equivariant $\mathit{C\ell}_{3}$ -modules. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem B.2.

Recall from (7.49a) that the Smith homomorphism $\mathrm{sm}_{V}\colon\Omega_{k}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\to\Omega_{k-3}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ belongs to a long exact sequence whose third term is spin $c$ bordism:

$$ \dotsb\to\Omega_{2}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\overset{\mathrm{sm}_{V}}{\to}\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\to\Omega_{3}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\dots $$

From Stong [Sto68, Chapter XI] we know $\Omega_{3}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}=0$ and $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , from Freed-Hopkins [FH21, Theorem 9.97] we know $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ , and from Wan-Wang [WW19, §5.5.3] we know $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ and $\Omega_{2}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ is torsion. Plugging this into (B.11), we see that $\mathrm{sm}_{V}$ is surjective.

Wan-Wang’s argument implies that the map $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}\to\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ choosing the trivial $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle is an isomorphism, so the generator of $\Omega_{1}^{\mathrm{Spin}}(B\mathrm{SO}(3))$ is any nonbounding spin $1$ -manifold with trivial $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle. Hu [Hu23, Appendix A] shows that $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ and $S^{4}$ generate $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}$ , where $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ has spinh structure induced from its spin $c$ structure via the standard inclusion $\mathrm{U}(1)\cong\mathrm{SO}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ , and $S^{4}$ has spinh structure whose principal $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle $V\to S^{4}$ is induced from the tautological quaternionic line bundle on $\mathbb{HP}^{1}\cong S^{4}$ : this has an associated $\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ -bundle, and we quotient by $\{\pm 1\}$ to get an $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ -bundle. In particular, $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ is in the image of $\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{c}}\to\Omega_{4}^{\mathrm{Spin}^{h}}$ , so because $\mathrm{sm}_{V}$ is surjective, $\mathrm{sm}_{V}(S^{4},V)$ must be $S_{\mathit{nb}}^{1}$ with trivial map to $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ , proving the first part of the theorem.

Because $H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{3}(S^{4};\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish, the $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}/2$ cohomology Euler classes of $V$ are zero. Therefore any null-homologous $1$ -manifold in $S^{4}$ (i.e. any closed, oriented $1$ -manifold mapping to $S^{4}$ ) is a smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e(V)$ . Most of these manifolds, such as the standard $S^{1}\subset S^{4}$ , can be given a nonbounding spin structure, but the empty submanifold cannot, even though it is Poincaré dual to $e(V)$ . This proves the second part of the theorem.

As discussed above, the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro map is $7$ -connected, and therefore for discussing degree- $3$ spin cobordism of $S^{4}$ , we may use $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology without losing information. The Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequence quickly implies

$$ \mathit{ko}^{*}(S^{4})\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[z]/(z^{2}),\ \lvert z\rvert=4. $$

In particular, $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ , generated by $\eta z$ .

The spinor bundle of $V$ is the quaternionic line bundle associated to the identification $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . Since $V$ came from the identification $S^{4}\cong\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ , the spinor bundle of $V$ is the tautological quaternionic line bundle $L_{\mathbb{H}}\to\mathbb{HP}^{1}$ . This is classified by the inclusion $j\colon\mathbb{HP}^{1}\to\mathbb{HP}^{\infty}\simeq B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ as the $4$ -skeleton; considering the map of Atiyah-Hirzebruch spectral sequences for $\mathit{ko}$ -cohomology induced by $j$ shows that $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ pulls back by $j$ to $z\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(S^{4})$ . Thus by Corollary B.5, $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)=\eta z\neq 0$ in $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})$ .

Because $\mathit{ko}^{3}(S^{4})$ has only one nonzero element, the Poincaré dual of the nonzero element must be the unique nonzero element $x$ of $\mathit{ko}_{1}(S^{4})\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Pulling back to spin bordism, the same argument we made for $B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ shows that the smooth representatives of $x$ are precisely the nonbounding spin $1$ -manifolds with null-bordant map to $S^{4}$ —and composing with the map $S^{4}\to B\mathrm{SO}(3)$ classifying $V$ , we have shown that every smooth representative of the Poincaré dual of $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)$ (hence also the spin cobordism Euler class) represents the image of $(S^{4},V)$ under the Smith homomorphism. ∎

In the remainder of this appendix, we give another proof of Corollary B.5. This second proof uses more homotopy theory, but no equivariant methods; as such, we think the two proofs complement each other.

#### Lemma B.13 (Greenlees-May [GM95, §15]).

There is a $\mathit{ko}$ -module equivalence

$$ \mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\simeq\mathit{ko}\vee\bigvee_{n\geq 0}\Sigma^{4n+2}\mathit{ku}. $$

#### Lemma B.15.

There is a $\mathit{ko}$ -module equivalence

$$ \mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{n\geq 0}\Sigma^{4n}\mathit{ko}. $$

#### Proof.

Recall that in (7.43), we showed using a variant of the proof of Lemma 7.26 that there’s an $MT\mathrm{Spin}$ -module equivalence

$$ MT\mathrm{Spin}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}\simeq\bigvee_{n\geq 0}\Sigma^{4n}MT\mathrm{Spin}. $$

The result immediately follows by applying $\text{--}\wedge_{MT\mathrm{Spin}}\mathit{ko}$ to both sides, where the algebra map $MT\mathrm{Spin}\to\mathit{ko}$ is the Atiyah-Bott-Shapiro orientation [ABS64, Joa04]. ∎

#### Remark B.18.

Analogues of Lemmas B.13 and B.15 for the periodic theory $\mathit{KO}$ and its generalizations to the higher real $K$ -theories $\mathit{EO}_{\Gamma}$ are known: see Bousfield [Bou90], Meier [Mei17, Theorem 2.8], Chatham [Cha20, Theorems 5.13 and 5.14], Bhattacharya-Chatham [BC22, Main Theorem 1.7], and Chatham-Hu-Opie [CHO24, Example 2.10].

#### Definition B.19.

Recall the complexification map $c\colon\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{ku}$ . The cofiber of $c$ is a map $R\colon\mathit{ku}\to\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ko}$ , denoted realification.

As $\mathit{ku}\not\simeq\mathit{ko}\vee\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ko}$ , the third map in the cofiber sequence begun by $c$ and $R$ must be nontrivial in

$$ \pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathit{ko}}(\Sigma\mathit{ko},\mathit{ko})\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\mathbb{S}}(\Sigma\mathbb{S},\mathit{ko})\cong\pi_{1}\mathit{ko}\cong\mathbb{Z}/2, $$

so must be the unique nontrivial class, namely the Hopf map $\eta\colon\Sigma\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{ko}$ . That is, we have found the Wood cofiber sequence

$$ \mathit{ko}\overset{c}{\longrightarrow}\mathit{ku}\overset{R}{\longrightarrow}\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ko}\overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow}\Sigma\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\dotsb $$

which we identified as a Smith cofiber sequence in Example 7.15.

Recall from Example 7.59 that the unit sphere bundle inside the tautological rank- $3$ vector bundle $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ is homotopy equivalent to the map $B\mathrm{Spin}(2)\to B\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ , which can be identified via accidental isomorphisms to the map $B\mathrm{U}(1)\to B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ given by the inclusion of a maximal torus. Choose for concreteness the standard maximal torus, given by the map $\mathrm{U}(1)\to\mathrm{SU}(2)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ defined by

$$ i\colon z\mapsto\begin{bmatrix}z&0\\
0&z^{-1}\end{bmatrix}. $$

Thus there is a Smith cofiber sequence

$$ \mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\overset{i_{*}}{\longrightarrow}\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}\overset{\frown e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)}{\longrightarrow}\mathit{ko}\wedge\Sigma^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))^{V_{3}-3}, $$

which is the cofiber sequence in Example 7.51 smashed with $\mathit{ko}$ .3535 35 In [DDK+25, §IV.F], we computed the Anderson dual long exact sequence in low degrees. This sequence is also studied, and placed in context, in Example 7.51.

Since $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ is spin, the Thom isomorphism identifies the third term in this sequence with $\Sigma^{3}\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}$ .

#### Proposition B.24.

The identifications in Lemmas B.13 and B.15 may be chosen to produce the following identifications of $\mathit{ko}$ -module homomorphisms.

$$  $$

- (1) The map $i_{*}\colon\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}\to\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}$ is the direct sum of the maps (B.25a)

$$ \Sigma^{4n+2}R\colon\Sigma^{4n+2}\mathit{ku}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{4n}\mathit{ko}, $$

together with the identity $\mathit{ko}\to\mathit{ko}$ on the basepoint.

- (2) The fiber of $i_{*}$ , which is a map $y\colon\mathit{ko}\wedge\Sigma^{2}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}\to\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{U}(1))_{+}$ , is the direct sum of the maps (B.25b)

$$ \Sigma^{4n+2}c\colon\Sigma^{4n+2}\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{4n+2}\mathit{ku}. $$

- (3) The map $\frown e^{\mathit{ko}}(V)\colon\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}\to\Sigma^{3}\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}$ is the direct sum of the maps (B.25c)

$$ \Sigma^{4n-1}\eta\colon\Sigma^{4n}\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{4n-1}\mathit{ko}, $$

together with the zero map on the copy of $\mathit{ko}$ in degree $0$ .

#### Proof.

Using the Wood cofiber sequence (B.21), any one of these three results implies the other two; we will prove (2).

Restricted to $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ , $y$ is a map

$$ y|_{\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}}\colon\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\mathit{ko}\vee\bigvee_{\ell\geq 0}\Sigma^{4\ell+2}\mathit{ku}. $$

We will show that it is possible to choose the equivalences in Lemmas B.13 and B.15 to make $y$ “diagonal,” i.e. after composing to the projection onto each summand of (B.26) except $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ku}$ , $y|_{\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}}$ is trivial. We know that the “diagonal terms,” i.e. the maps obtained by restricting $y$ to $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ and then projecting to the $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ku}$ summand in the codomain, must be $\pm c$ , because this is the only choice compatible with base change along $\mathit{ko}\to H\mathbb{Z}$ inducing maps on $\mathbb{Z}$ cohomology which are isomorphisms in those degrees: this is because

$$ \pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathit{ko}}(\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko},\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ku})\cong\pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathbb{S}}(\mathbb{S},\mathit{ku})\cong\pi_{0}\mathit{ku}\cong\mathbb{Z} $$

and $c$ is a generator; thus we must obtain either $c$ or $-c$ on the equal-degree summand.

The map out of $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ is trivial when projected to the $\mathit{ko}$ in degree $0$ , because we need that $\Sigma^{0}\mathit{ko}$ summand to map to the degree- $0$ $\mathit{ko}$ summand in the cofiber $\mathit{ko}\wedge(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))_{+}$ , because that map arose from a basepoint-preserving map of spaces. In the rest of the proof, we will address the $\Sigma^{4\ell+2}\mathit{ku}$ summands.

A map of $\mathit{ko}$ -modules $\Sigma^{m}\mathit{ko}\to\Sigma^{n}\mathit{ku}$ is equivalent data to a map of spectra $\Sigma^{m}\mathbb{S}\to\Sigma^{n}\mathit{ku}$ , which is classified by $\pi_{n}(\mathit{ku})$ . Since $\mathit{ku}$ is connective, all “off-diagonal terms” vanish unless $4k+2\geq 4\ell+2$ ; therefore for our $\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ summand we may restrict to the map

$$ y\colon\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ko}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}\longrightarrow\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ku}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ku}. $$

We may therefore describe $y$ as a $(k+1)\times(k+1)$ matrix. Connectivity of $\mathit{ku}$ implies this matrix is upper triangular.

We saw in (B.27) that if $m\geq\ell$ , then $\pi_{0}\mathrm{Map}_{\mathit{ko}}(\Sigma^{4m+2}\mathit{ko},\Sigma^{4\ell+2}\mathit{ku})\cong\pi_{2(m-\ell)}\mathit{ku}\cong\mathbb{Z}$ ; tracing through the identifications there, we learn that this $\mathbb{Z}$ of maps is the set of scalar multiples of the map $b^{2(m-\ell)}c$ , where $b\colon\Sigma^{2}\mathit{ku}\to\mathit{ku}$ is the connective version of the Bott periodicity map. Therefore there are integers $\lambda_{ij}$ for $1\leq i<j\leq k+1$ such that the map (B.28) is given by the following upper triangular matrix:

$$ \begin{bmatrix}\pm c&\lambda_{12}b^{2}c&\lambda_{13}b^{4}c&\dotsb&\lambda_{1(k+1)}b^{2k}c\\
&\pm c&\lambda_{23}b^{2}c&\dotsb&\lambda_{2(k+1)}b^{2k-2}c\\
&&\ddots&\ddots&\vdots\\
&&&\pm c&\lambda_{k(k+1)}b^{2}c\\
&&&&\pm c\end{bmatrix}. $$

This matrix can clearly be row-reduced over $\mathit{ko}_{*}$ to $c\cdot\mathrm{Id}$ , and the requisite row operations correspond to automorphisms of $\mathit{ko}\vee\dotsb\vee\Sigma^{4k+2}\mathit{ko}$ . The row operations are compatible with adding on more summands by increasing $k$ , so we may conclude. ∎

#### Lemma B.30 (Bruner-Greenlees (see [BPR23, Theorem 3.8])).

Recall $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ from Proposition B.4. There is an isomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathit{ko}_{*}[x]$ , where $\lvert x\rvert=4$ ,3636 36 Here we use polynomial notation only for conciseness; we have not defined any ring structure on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ . such that the $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ -module structure on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ is the one uniquely specified by

$$ p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\frown x^{k}=x^{k-1}. $$

Finally, we can calculate the $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler class!

#### Proof of Corollary B.5.

It suffices to work universally with the tautological bundle $V_{3}\to B\mathrm{Spin}(3)$ ; the spinor bundle is the tautological quaternionic line bundle associated to $\mathrm{Spin}(3)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ , and so $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}_{V_{3}})$ is the class we called $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ in Proposition B.4.

By Proposition B.24,

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{3})\frown x^{k}=\eta x^{k-1}, $$

where we define $x^{-1}=0$ for convenience.3737 37 As we have not been careful about explicit choices of isomorphisms, there could be a sign factor in the choice of $x^{k}$ , but since $2\eta=0$ , the possible sign error goes away. A general element of $\mathit{ko}^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ is of the form

$$ \sum_{k\geq 0}\eta(p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}})^{k}w^{k-1}. $$

We know how $\eta$ and $w^{k-1}$ act on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ because the $\mathit{ko}$ -theory cap product is linear over $\mathit{ko}^{*}$ . We know how $p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ acts on $\mathit{ko}_{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1))$ thanks to Lemma B.30. Using these, we can see that the only class of the form (B.33) whose cap product matches that of $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{3})$ in (B.32) is $\eta p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}$ .

Finally, we have to check that $e^{\mathbb{Z}}(V_{3})$ and $e^{\mathbb{Z}/2}(V_{3})$ both vanish. $B\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ is $3$ -connected, so $H^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1);\mathbb{Z})$ and $H^{3}(B\mathrm{Sp}(1);\mathbb{Z}/2)$ both vanish. ∎

#### Remark B.34 (Euler classes of low-rank spin vector bundles).

For $2\leq n\leq 6$ , $\mathrm{Spin}(n)$ participates in an accidental isomorphism with another Lie group, and one can run similar arguments to compute $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler classes of other low-rank vector bundles as corollaries of Atiyah’s Theorem B.3.

- (1) If $L$ is a real line bundle with spin structure, $e^{\mathit{ko}}(L)=0$ , because $e^{\mathit{ko}}$ pulls back from the twisted Euler class over $B\mathrm{SO}(1)=*$ ; see, e.g., Crabb [Cra91, Corollary 3.37(i)].

- (2) If $V_{2}$ has rank $2$ , one can use the accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(2)\cong\mathrm{U}(1)$ and the fact that the map $c\colon\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{U}(1))\to\mathit{ku}^{*}(B\mathrm{U}(1))$ is injective [BG10, §5.2] to show that $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{2})$ is determined by $e^{\mathit{ku}}(V)$ , hence also by $e^{K}(V)$ , the image in periodic $K$ -theory. In particular, $V_{2}$ acquires the structure of a complex line bundle, and there is a formula for the $K$ -theory Euler classes of complex vector bundles, e.g. in Bott [Bot69, (7.2)].

- (4) If $V_{4}\to X$ has rank $4$ , its spinor bundle factors as $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}^{+}\oplus\mathcal{S}^{-}$ , where the two factors $\mathcal{S}^{\pm}$ are quaternionic line bundles associated to the two factors of $\phi\colon\mathrm{Spin}(4)\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{Sp}(1)\times\mathrm{Sp}(1)$ . There is a choice of $\phi$ such that (B.35)

$$ e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{4})=p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}^{+})-p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}(\mathcal{S}^{-})\in\mathit{ko}^{4}(X). $$

- (5) There is an accidental isomorphism $\mathrm{Spin}(5)\cong\mathrm{Sp}(2)$ , and $\mathit{ko}^{*}(B\mathrm{Sp}(2))\cong\mathit{ko}^{*}[[p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}},p_{2}^{\mathbb{H}}]]$ with $\lvert p_{1}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=4$ and $\lvert p_{2}^{\mathbb{H}}\rvert=8$ (see [DM79, §2] or [BG10, Theorem 5.3.5]). Therefore $\mathit{ko}^{5}(B\mathrm{Sp}(2))\cong 0$ , so for any rank- $5$ spin vector bundle $V_{5}$ , $e^{\mathit{ko}}(V_{5})=0$ ; see, e.g., Crabb [Cra91, Corollary 3.37(i)].

#### Remark B.36.

We saw above that for twisted spin bordism, the $\mathit{ko}$ -theoretic Euler class suffices to approximate the cobordism Euler class. For other tangential structures, one may need more or less information.

- • Unoriented bordism decomposes as a sum of shifts of mod $2$ homology, and this splitting is compatible with the Smith homomorphism. Therefore in this setting, one can use the $\mathbb{Z}/2$ -cohomology Euler class.

- • Wall [Wal60] showed that $MT\mathrm{SO}$ , localized at $2$ , splits as a sum of shifts of $H\mathbb{Z}$ and $H\mathbb{Z}/2$ . Therefore when one studies Smith homomorphisms for twisted oriented bordism, the $\mathbb{Z}$ -cohomology Euler class will be accurate up to odd-primary torsion. On odd-primary torsion, oriented and spin bordism coincide, so in that setting one can use $\mathit{ko}$ -Euler classes for twisted oriented bordism.

- • Analogously to spin and $\mathit{ko}$ , one can use $\mathit{ku}$ -theory Euler classes for twisted spin $c$ bordism Smith homomorphisms.

# Relative Langlands duality for linear periods

**Authors:** Tsao-Hsien Chen Address: School of Mathematics, University of Minnesota, Twin cities, Minneapolis, MN 55455 Email address: chenth@umn.edu , Sanath K. Devalapurkar Address: School of Mathematics. Institute for Advanced Study 1 Einstein Drive Princeton, New Jersey 08540 Email address: skdevalapurkar@gmail.com , Mark Macerato Address: School of Mathematics, University of Minnesota, Twin cities, Minneapolis, MN 55455 Email address: macer008@umn.edu and David Nadler Address: Department of Mathematics, UC Berkeley, Evans Hall, Berkeley, CA 9472 Email address: nadler@math.berkeley.edu

## Abstract

We prove relative Langlands duality for $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ . These symmetric spaces arise in the setting of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet when $p=q$ , and exhibit non-tempered behavior when $q>p+1$ . Via the real-symmetric correspondence, we establish a derived Satake equivalence for the real group $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , and use it to obtain a constructible realization of coherent sheaves on Kato’s exotic nilpotent cones. Along the way, we describe the dual variety of $X$ in terms of the Whittaker cotangent bundle and regular centralizers, viewed as Coulomb branches.

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1. Relative Langlands duality

The relative Langlands program of Ben-Zvi, Sakellaridis and Venkatesh [BZSV] proposes geometric mechanisms for observed and conjectural relations between periods and L-functions.

A fundamental conjecture in the program predicts that given a complex reductive group $G$ , with dual group $\check{G}$ , and a homogeneous spherical $G$ -variety $X$ , there exists a (graded) Hamiltonian $\check{G}$ -variety $\check{M}$ with moment map $\mu:\check{M}\to\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ equipped with a commuting $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action satisfying $\mu(t\cdot m)=t^{2}\mu(m)$ , and a relative derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash} $$

On the left or automorphic side, $\mathfrak{L}X$ is the formal loop space of $X$ , $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ is the formal arc space of $G$ , and $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ is the bounded constructible dg-derived category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant sheaves on $\mathfrak{L}X$ . On the right or spectral/Galois side, $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ is the sheared dg-category of $\check{G}$ -equivariant perfect dg-modules over the ring of functions on $\check{M}$ viewed as a dg-algebra with trivial differential and grading given by the $\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -action. The shearing notation and the shifted vector spaces used below are defined in Section 4.2; the parity convention is specified in Section 4.4.

Moreover, the relative derived Satake equivalence (1) should be compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

where $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}=\mathfrak{L}G/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ is the affine Grassmannian, $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})$ acts on $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ by convolution, and $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2])$ acts on $\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{M})^{\hskip-1.63885pt\fatslash}$ by tensor product through $\mu$ .

### 1.2. Linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet

An important instance of relative duality is the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet [FJ]: here one takes $G=GL_{2p}$ , so with dual group $\check{G}=GL_{2p}$ , and studies $X=GL_{2p}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{p})$ with expected dual

$$ \check{M}=GL_{2p}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[1]) $$

$$ \check{M}/\check{G}=(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[1])/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} $$

Similar phenomena can be observed more generally, when one takes $G=GL_{p+q}$ , $q\geq p$ , so with dual group $\check{G}=GL_{p+q}$ , and studies $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ with expected dual

$$ \check{M}=GL_{p+q}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

$$ \check{M}/\check{G}=(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p})/\mathrm{Sp}_{2p} $$

In the associated-bundle presentation the grading also acts on the group factor by $g\mapsto g\lambda(t)^{-1}$ , with $\lambda$ as in (8); after quotienting by $\check{G}$ , only the displayed fiber degrees remain. When $p=q$ , the final $GL_{q-p}$ quotient factor is a point. Note this is tempered if and only if $q=p$ or $q=p+1$ .

Our main result is a relative derived Satake equivalence in this setting:

#### Theorem 1.2.1.

(see Theorem 4.2.1) For $G=GL_{p+q}$ , $q\geq p$ , and $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ , there is a relative derived Satake equivalence of dg-categories

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

Within the above derived Satake equivalence, we also find an abelian equivalence. According to [CN, Section 8.4], the category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}^{b}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ admits a perverse $t$ -structure. We denote the corresponding category of perverse sheaves by $\mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ .

#### Theorem 1.2.2.

(see Theorem 4.4.1) There is an equivalence of abelian category

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}))\ \ \ \ \ p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ p\neq q.\end{cases} $$

### 1.3. Derived Satake equivalence for $U(p,q)$

A key feature of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet, and more generally of $G=GL_{p+q}$ acting on $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ is that $X$ is a symmetric space, i.e. $K=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ is the fixed-points of an involution $\theta$ of $G$ . Among many consequences, this allows one to reinterpret the relative derived Satake equivalence of Theorem 1.2.1 in terms of the unitary group $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , which is quasi-split if and only if $q=p$ or $q=p+1$ . Following [CN] and recalled as Proposition 2.4.5 below, the automorphic side admits a natural equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\cong D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}) $$

where $\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}=\mathfrak{L}U(p,q)/\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)$ is the real affine Grassmannian of $U(p,q)$ . Moreover, the equivalence (2) is compatible with natural actions of the derived Satake category.

So the relative derived Satake equivalence of Theorem 1.2.1 can be restated as a real derived Satake equivalence:

#### Theorem 1.3.1 (see Theorem 4.2.1).

For $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ there is a real derived Satake equivalence of dg-categories

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}(\wedge^{2}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[2]\times T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p}[q-p+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}^{*}_{q-p}[2]\sslash GL_{q-p}) $$

compatible with the natural monoidal actions under the derived Satake equivalence

$$ D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}_{G})\cong\mathrm{Perf}^{\check{G}}(\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}[2]) $$

According to [N], there is natural perverse $t$ -structure on $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})$ and we denote by $\mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})$ the corresponding category of perverse sheaves.

#### Theorem 1.3.2.

(see Theorem 4.4.1) There is an equivalence of abelian category

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}))\ \ \ \ \ p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ p\neq q.\end{cases} $$

### 1.4. Whittaker cotangent bundles and regular centralizers

Another key feature of the linear period of Friedberg–Jacquet, and more generally of $G=GL_{p+q}$ acting on $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ is that $K=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ is a Levi subgroup of $G$ . The work of the third author [M] suggests the alternative description of the dual variety $\check{M}$ as the affine closure of the Whittaker cotangent bundle

$$ \check{M}\cong\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})} $$

here $T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})$ is the Hamiltonian reduction of $T^{*}\check{G}$ by a maximal unipotent subgroup $\check{U}=[\check{B},\check{B}]\subset\check{G}$ at $-d\psi_{\check{K}}$ for the right action $g\mapsto gu^{-1}$ , where $\psi_{\check{K}}:\check{U}\to\mathbb{G}_{a}$ is an additive character nontrivial precisely on the simple roots of the dual Levi $\check{K}=GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ (see Section 3.4 for more details).

On the other hand, a recent general result of Ginzburg [Gi] suggests another description of the dual variety in terms of regular centerlizers group schemes:

$$ \check{M}\cong\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}} $$

here the right hand side is the affine closure of the quotient $\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}$ , where $J_{\check{G}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}$ , $J_{\check{K}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}$ are the group schemes of regular centralizers, and $\pi:\mathfrak{c}_{\check{K}}\to\mathfrak{c}_{\check{G}}$ is the natural projection (see Section 3.5 for more details).

Indeed, we prove the isomorphisms (3) and (4), which is the key step in our approach to Relative Langlands duality for linear periods:

#### Theorem 1.4.1 (see Theorem 3.6.1).

There are $\check{G}\times\mathbb{G}_{m}$ -equivariant isomorphisms of affine varieties over $\check{\mathfrak{g}}^{*}$ in the following commutative diagram

$$ \textstyle{\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\simeq} \scriptstyle{\simeq} \textstyle{\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\check{M}} $$

In fact, the isomorphism $\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\cong\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ in Theorem 1.4.1 follows from the work in [Ga, M], which is valid when $\check{K}$ is a general Levi subgroups (not necessarily symmetric or spherical), and the main step in the proof is the isomorphism (3). The proof uses a generalization of Kostant theorem, see Section 3.7, and a Lagrangian correspondence between $T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})$ and $\check{M}$ , see Section 27.

Since $\check{M}$ is smooth, as a corollary of the theorem we obtain the following:

#### Corollary 1.4.2 (see Corollary 3.6.2).

The affine closures $\overline{T^{*}_{\psi_{\check{K}}}(\check{G}/\check{U})}\cong\overline{(\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}})/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ are smooth.

#### Remark 1.4.3.

It is proved in [Gi, Corollary 3.1.6] that the affine closure $\overline{\check{G}\times J_{\check{K}}/\pi^{*}J_{\check{G}}}$ for general connected reductive subgroup $\check{K}\subset\check{G}$ is an irreducible normal variety. However, the smoothness of the affine closures in setting of Levi symmetric subgroup $\check{K}=\mathrm{GL}_{p}\times\mathrm{GL}_{q}$ was unexpected at least by the authors.

### 1.6. Hermitian symmetric spaces

The symmetric space $X=GL_{p+q}/(GL_{p}\times GL_{q})$ considered in this paper is a particular example of a Hermitian symmetric space. In forthcoming work [CDMN], we expect to establish Relative Langlands duality for Hermitian symmetric spaces with no roots of type $N$ . Modulo central factors, the Hermitian symmetric spaces under consideration are as follows:

| $X=G/K$ | Rank |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{GL}_{2r+m}/(\mathrm{GL}_{r}\times\mathrm{GL}_{r+m})$ | $r$ |
| $\mathrm{PSO}_{2n}/\mathrm{GSO}_{2n-2}$ | $2$ |
| $\mathrm{SO}_{4r}/\mathrm{GL}_{2r}$ | $r$ |
| $\mathrm{SO}_{4r+2}/\mathrm{GL}_{2r+1}$ | $r$ |
| $E_{6}/\mathrm{GSO}_{10}$ | $2$ |
| $E_{7}/GE_{6}$ | $3$ |

A striking feature of the Hermitian symmetric case is that, after forgetting the gradings, all of the corresponding dual varieties $\check{M}$ are of the form

$$ {\check{G}}\times^{\mathrm{Sp}(V)}(T^{\ast}(V)\times\wedge^{2}(V)\times\mathbf{A}^{a_{X}}) $$

where $V$ is a vector space of dimension $2r$ and $a_{X}$ is the dimension of the remaining affine factor. For the linear periods considered here, $r=p$ and $a_{X}=q-p$ .

## 2. Constructible side

Throughout, sheaves have complex coefficients, and $\mathrm{Rep}(H)$ denotes finite-dimensional algebraic representations of a complex algebraic group $H$ . We use $D^{b}$ for the bounded, finite-rank constructible category and $\mathrm{Perv}$ for its perverse heart. The cocomplete categories $D$ and their compact objects are distinguished below in Section 2.3.

### 2.1. Real groups and symmetric spaces

Let $G=GL_{N}$ be the complex general linear group of rank $N$ . Let $T$ be the diagonal maximal torus and $B=TU$ be the Borel subgroup of upper triangular matrices.

Fix integers $1\leq p\leq q$ and put $N=p+q$ . Consider the following matrix

$$ I_{p,q}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&J_{p}\\
0&I_{q-p}&0\\
J_{p}&0&0\end{pmatrix} $$

where $I_{q-p}$ is the identity matrix of size $q-p$ and $J_{p}$ is the permutation matrix with $1$ ’s on the anti diagonal and $0$ ’s elsewhere. Consider the involution $\theta:G\to G$ given by $\theta(g)=I_{p,q}g(I_{p,q})^{-1}$ . The fixed point subgroup $K=G^{\theta}$ is a Levi symmetric subgroup of $G$ isomorphic to $K\cong GL_{p}\times GL_{q}$ . We denote by $X=G/K$ the associated symmetric space.

The block upper triangular subgroup

$$ P=\begin{pmatrix}B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}&*&*\\
0&GL_{q-p}&*\\
0&0&B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}\end{pmatrix} $$

is a $\theta$ -split minimal parabolic subgroup, where $B_{p}^{\mathrm{}}\subset GL_{p}$ is the upper triangular Borel. Its Levi subgroup is

$$ L=P\cap\theta(P)=\begin{pmatrix}GL_{1}^{p}&0&0\\
0&GL_{q-p}&0\\
0&0&GL_{1}^{p}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The subtorus $A=\{t\in T|\theta(t)=t^{-1}\}^{\circ}\subset T$ is a maximal $\theta$ -split torus consisting of diagonal matrices of the form

$$ \text{diag}(a_{1},...,a_{p},1,...,1,a_{p}^{-1},...,a_{1}^{-1}) $$

We have $L=Z_{G}(A)$ and $P=LU_{P}=MAU_{P}$ where $U_{P}$ is the unipotent radical of $P$ and $M=Z_{K}(A)$ . We see that $X$ is quasi-split (but non-split) if and only if $p=q$ or $p+1=q$ .

We write $\Lambda_{T}=X_{*}(T)$ for the coweight lattice and $\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ for the dominant coweights with respect to $(T,B)$ . Let $2\rho\in X^{*}(T)$ be the sum of the positive roots. The real coweight lattice is $\Lambda_{A}=X_{*}(A)$ , with $\Lambda_{A}^{+}=\Lambda_{A}\cap\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ . Under the coordinate identifications $X_{*}(T)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{N}$ and $X^{*}(T)\cong\mathbf{Z}^{N}$ , we have

$$ 2\rho=(N-1,N-3,\ldots,-N+3,-N+1). $$

The elements of $\Lambda_{A}$ are the tuples

$$ (\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{p},0,\ldots,0,-\lambda_{p},\ldots,-\lambda_{1}). $$

We have an embedding $\tau:X\to G$ sending $x=gK$ to $g\theta(g)^{-1}$ which induces an isomorphism $\tau:X\cong Q=\{g\in G|\theta(g)=g^{-1}\}^{\circ}$ between $X$ and the neutral component of the $\theta$ anti-fixed points in $G$ . We denote by $\iota_{A}:A\to Q\cong X$ the natural embedding.

Consider the conjugation $\eta_{c}:G\to G$ given by $\eta_{c}(g)=(\bar{g}^{t})^{-1}$ with fixed points subgroup $G_{c}=G^{\eta_{c}}=U(N)$ the compact unitary group. Consider the conjugation $\eta:G\to G$ given by $\eta(g)=I_{p,q}(\bar{g}^{-1})^{t}I_{p,q}^{-1}$ . The fixed point subgroup $G^{\eta}$ is a real form of $G$ , denote by $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,q)$ , known as the unitary group of signature $(p,q)$ . Consider the intersections $P_{\mathbf{R}}=P\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , $L_{\mathbf{R}}=L\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , and $U_{P,\mathbf{R}}=U_{P}\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ , etc. The intersection $P_{\mathbf{R}}=P\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the minimal parabolic subgroup with Iwasawa decomposition $P_{\mathbf{R}}=M_{\mathbf{R}}A_{\mathbf{R}}U_{P,\mathbf{R}}$ . The intersection $K_{c}=K\cap G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is a maximal compact subgroup isomorphic to the product $K_{c}\cong U(p)\times U(q)$ of unitary groups.

### 2.2. Loop spaces and affine Grassmannians

Let $\mathfrak{L}G$ and $\mathfrak{L}K$ denote the loop groups of $G$ and $K$ , respectively. We also have the arc subgroups $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G\subseteq\mathfrak{L}G$ and $\mathfrak{L}^{+}K\subseteq\mathfrak{L}K$ . Let $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}=\mathfrak{L}G/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ and $\mathrm{Gr}_{K}=\mathfrak{L}K/\mathfrak{L}^{+}K$ be the corresponding affine Grassmannians. We abbreviate $\mathrm{Gr}=\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . There is a natural closed immersion $\iota_{K}:\mathrm{Gr}_{K}\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . Let $\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ be the real loop group and $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}\subseteq\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ its arc subgroup. The quotient $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}=\mathfrak{L}G_{\mathbf{R}}/\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is the real affine Grassmannian, a real form of the ind-scheme $\mathrm{Gr}_{G}$ . For any $\lambda\in\Lambda_{T}^{+}$ (resp. $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ ) we denote by $\mathrm{Gr}^{\lambda}\subset\mathrm{Gr}$ (resp. $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}\subset\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ ) the $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -orbit (resp. $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ ) through $t^{\lambda}$ . We have $\mathrm{Gr}=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}_{T}}\mathrm{Gr}^{\lambda}$ and $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda^{+}_{A}}\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ .

Let $\mathfrak{L}X$ be the loop space of $X$ . The embedding $\iota_{A}:A\to X$ of the $\theta$ -split torus gives rise to an embedding $\Lambda_{A}\to\mathfrak{L}X$ sending $\lambda$ to $x^{\lambda}=\iota_{A}(t^{\lambda})$ . Let $\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}=\mathfrak{L}^{+}G\cdot x^{\lambda}$ be the $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -orbit through $x^{\lambda}$ . It is known that $\mathfrak{L}X=\bigsqcup_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}}\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}$ and $\overline{\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}}=\bigsqcup_{\mu\in\Lambda_{A}^{+},\mu\leq\lambda}\mathfrak{L}X^{\mu}$ (see, e.g., [CY, Proposition 17 and Theorem 18]).

### 2.3. Real and relative Satake categories

Let $(D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}),*)$ be the co-complete monoidal dg category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant constructible complexes on $\mathrm{Gr}$ with monoidal structure given by the convolution product: $F,F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ and $F\star F^{\prime}=m_{!}(F\tilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime})$ , where $m:\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathrm{Gr}\to\mathrm{Gr}$ is the natural action map and $F\tilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathrm{Gr})$ is the twisted product of $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ . It is known that $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ is compactly generated and we denote by $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})^{c}$ the subcategory of compact objects. The equivariant derived category $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ coincides with the subcategories of locally compact objects11 1 An object $F$ is called locally compact if its image under the forgetful functor $\mathrm{For}:D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\to D(\mathrm{Gr})$ is compact. and we denote by $\text{Ind}(D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr}))$ the ind-completion of $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ . We denote by $(D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}),*),$ etc, the corresponding monoidal categories for $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . We will call the categories $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ , etc (resp. $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ , etc) the complex Satake categories for $G$ (resp. real Satake categories for $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ ).

Let $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ be the co-complete dg category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant constructible complexes on $\mathfrak{L}X$ . Denote by $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)^{c}$ , $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}^{b}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ , and $\mathrm{Ind}(D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X))$ for the corresponding categories of compact objects, locally compact objects, and the ind-completion of the latter, respectively. We have a natural action of the complex Satake category

$$ *:D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\times D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)\to D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X) $$

given by $F\star F^{\prime}=a_{!}(F\widetilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime})$ where $a:\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathfrak{L}X\to\mathfrak{L}X$ is the action map and $F\widetilde{\boxtimes}F^{\prime}\in D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}G\times^{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}\mathfrak{L}X)$ is the twisted product of $F$ and $F^{\prime}$ . We will call the above category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathfrak{L}X)$ , etc, the relative Satake categories.

### 2.4. Hecke actions

Let $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}\to\mathbf{C}$ be the Beilinson-Drinfeld Grassmannian over the complex line classifying triples $(x,E,\phi)$ where $x\in\mathbf{C}$ , $E$ is a $G$ -bundle on $\mathbf{C}$ , and $\phi$ is a trivialization of $E$ on $\mathbf{C}\setminus\{\pm x\}$ . Consider the anti-holomorphic involution $\eta$ on $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}$ given by $\eta(x,E,\phi)=(-\bar{x},\eta^{*}E,\eta^{*}\phi)$ defines a real from $\mathrm{Gr}^{(2)}_{\mathbf{R}}\to i\mathbf{R}$ such that

$$ \textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}\times i\mathbf{R}_{>0}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{a} \textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{(2)}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{b} \textstyle{i\mathbf{R}_{>0}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{i\mathbf{R}} \textstyle{\{0\}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} $$

Consider the specialization functor

$$ \psi:D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\to D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})\ \ \ \psi(F)=b^{*}a_{*}(F\boxtimes\mathbf{C}_{i\mathbf{R}_{>0}}). $$

Let $\text{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\subset D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})$ be the category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -equivariant perverse sheaves on $\mathrm{Gr}$ . The geometric Satake equivalence says that there is an isomorphism of Tannakian category

$$ \text{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G}(\mathrm{Gr})\cong\text{Rep}(\check{G}) $$

where $\check{G}=GL_{N}$ is the dual group of $G$ such that the intersection cohomology complex $\text{IC}^{\lambda}$ for $\mathrm{Gr}^{\lambda}$ maps to the irreducible representations $V_{\lambda}$ of highest weight $\lambda$ . For $V\in\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})$ , write $\mathrm{IC}_{V}$ for its corresponding Satake sheaf. According to [N, Lemma 3.9.1], we have

$$ \dim_{\mathbf{R}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda})=\langle\lambda,2\rho\rangle=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}(N+1-2i)\lambda_{i}\in 2\mathbb{Z}. $$

Thus there is perverse $t$ -structure on the real Satake category $D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ given by the middle perversity function

$$ p_{\mathbf{R}}:\Lambda_{A}^{+}\to\mathbb{Z},\ \ \ p_{\mathbf{R}}(\lambda)=-\frac{\dim_{\mathbf{R}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda})}{2}=-\sum_{i=1}^{p}(N+1-2i)\lambda_{i} $$

We denote by $\text{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ the corresponding category of $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ -equivariant perverse sheaves on $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ .

The Hecke action of $\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})$ on the real Satake category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ , denoted again by $*$ , is defined as

$$ \mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})\times D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})\to D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})\ \ (V,F)\to V*F:=\psi(\mathrm{IC}_{V})*F $$

#### Proposition 2.4.1.

(1) The specialization functor $\psi$ , and hence the Hecke action, is monoidal. Moreover, the Hecke action is $t$ -exact with respect to the perverse $t$ -structure if and only if $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ is quasi-split, that is, when $G_{\mathbf{R}}=U(p,p)$ or $U(p,p+1)$ .

(2) The Hecke action of $\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})$ preserves semisimplicity, that is, it maps semi-simple objects to semi-simple objects.

#### Proof.

Part (1) is [N, Theorem 1.2.2 and Corollary 10.6.2] and Part (2) is [CN, Corollary 1.5]. ∎

We shall show that the real Satake category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ is generated by $\mathrm{IC}^{0}_{\mathbf{R}}$ under the Hecke action.

#### Lemma 2.4.2.

Any real dominant coweight $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ is of the form $\lambda=\mu-\theta(\mu)$ for some $\mu\in\Lambda_{T}$

#### Proof.

The involution $\theta$ sends a coweight $\mu=(a_{1},...,a_{p},b_{1},...,b_{q-p},c_{1},...c_{p})\in\Lambda_{T}\cong\mathbb{Z}^{N}$ to

$$ \theta(\mu)=(c_{p},...,c_{1},b_{1},...,b_{q-p},a_{p},...,a_{1}). $$

It follows that for any real dominant coweight $\lambda=(\lambda_{1},...\lambda_{p},0,...,0,-\lambda_{p},...,-\lambda_{1})\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ , we have $\lambda=\mu-\theta(\mu)$ where $\mu=(\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{p},0,...,0)\in\Lambda_{T}$ . The lemma follows. ∎

#### Lemma 2.4.3.

The $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ -stabilizers on $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}$ is connected.

#### Proof.

According to [N, Proposition 3.6.1], each $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}$ -orbit $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ is a $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ -equivariant vector bundle over a real flag manifold $G_{\mathbf{R}}/P_{\mathbf{R},\lambda}$ , where $P_{\mathbf{R},\lambda}$ is a real parabolic subgroup depending on $\lambda$ . Thus it suffices to check that $P_{\mathbf{R},\lambda}$ is connected. Since a real parabolic is connected if and only if its Levi subgroup is connected, we reduce to the latter assertion. The Levi subgroups of $G_{\mathbf{R}}$ are isomorphic to

$$ U(p-a,q-a)\times\prod_{i}GL_{n_{i}}(\mathbb{C}),\qquad a=\sum_{i}n_{i}\leq p, $$

which is connected. ∎

#### Proposition 2.4.4.

(1) The irreducible objects of $\mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ are given by the the intersection cohomology complex $\mathrm{IC}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ for $\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ , $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ .

(2) The real Satake category $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ is generated by $\mathrm{IC}_{\mathbf{R}}^{0}$ under the Hecke action of $\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})$

#### Proof.

Lemma 2.4.3 implies that $D_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}G_{\mathbf{R}}}(\mathrm{Gr}_{\mathbf{R}})$ is generated by $\mathrm{IC}$ -complexes $\mathrm{IC}_{\mathbf{R}}^{\lambda}$ and Lemma 2.4.2 together with [N, Corollary 10.6.2] implies, up to shifts, all the $\mathrm{IC}$ -complexes appear as a direct summand of $V\star\mathrm{IC}_{\mathbf{R}}^{0}$ for some $V\in\mathrm{Rep}(\check{G})$ . The corollary follows. ∎

It is shown in [CY, Theorem 3.6] that the collection of spherical orbits $\{\mathfrak{L}X^{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}}$ provides a placid stratification of $\mathfrak{L}X$ (see [CY, Appendix A] for a review of placidness). Recall the following real-symmetric equivalence [CN, Theorem 1.1]:

#### Proposition 2.4.5.
