### 4.4. Abelian equivalences

Put $\delta=q-p$ , $H=\check{G}_{X}=\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}$ , $V=\mathbb{A}^{2p}$ , and $W=T^{*}V=V\oplus V^{*}$ . Consider the dg algebras with zero differential

$$ \displaystyle\mathfrak{A}_{p,q} \displaystyle=\operatorname{Sym}^{*}\left(\wedge^{2}V[1]\oplus(\Pi^{\delta+1}W)[\delta]\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\delta}\mathbb{A}^{1}[2i-1]\right), \displaystyle\mathfrak{B}_{p,q} \displaystyle=\operatorname{Sym}^{*}\left(\wedge^{2}V[-2]\oplus(\Pi^{\delta+1}W)[-\delta-1]\oplus\bigoplus_{i=1}^{\delta}\mathbb{A}^{1}[-2i]\right). $$

Write $\mathfrak{A}=\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}$ and $\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}$ . Our convention is that $E[k]$ lies in cohomological degree $-k$ , and the symmetric algebras use the sign $(-1)^{ij+\epsilon\eta}$ for cohomological degrees $i,j$ and internal parities $\epsilon,\eta$ . All modules are left modules. Their internal parity is prescribed by the central element $(-I)^{\delta+1}\in H$ ; thus an independent parity shift does not give additional simple objects.

The algebra $\mathfrak{A}$ is finite-dimensional and nonpositive, while $\mathfrak{B}$ is polynomial with generators in strictly positive degrees and $\mathfrak{B}^{0}=\mathbb{C}$ . Let $D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})$ denote the category of equivariant dg modules with finite total cohomology, and let $D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod})$ be the thick subcategory generated by $\mathfrak{B}\otimes U$ for finite-dimensional $H$ -representations $U$ . Using the $H$ -equivariant self-dualities of $\wedge^{2}V$ and $W$ , Koszul duality gives

$$ \kappa:D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod})\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod}),\qquad M\longmapsto\mathbb{C}\overset{\mathbf{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathfrak{B}}M, $$

where the derived fiber carries its Koszul $\mathfrak{A}$ -action; see [BFGT, Section 3.8]. Equivalently, $\kappa$ is the inverse of $N\mapsto R\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathbb{C},N)$ under $\mathfrak{B}\simeq R\operatorname{End}_{\mathfrak{A}}(\mathbb{C})^{\mathrm{op}}$ .

The standard $t$ -structure on $D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})$ is bounded, with heart the finite-dimensional $H$ -equivariant $H^{0}(\mathfrak{A})$ -modules. Hence

$$ D^{H}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}\mathrm{-mod})^{\heartsuit}\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}W\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(H)),&p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(H),&p<q.\end{cases} $$

Recall from Theorem 4.2.1 the derived Satake equivalence

$$ \displaystyle\Phi^{b}:D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)}) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathrm{Perf}^{H}\left(\wedge^{2}V[2]\times W[\delta+1]\times\mathfrak{gl}_{\delta}^{*}[2]\sslash GL_{\delta}\right) \displaystyle\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{H}_{perf}(\mathfrak{B}\mathrm{-mod}) $$

#### Theorem 4.4.1.

The composed equivalence

$$ \kappa\circ\Phi^{b}:D^{b}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\xrightarrow{\sim}D^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}\mathrm{-mod}) $$

is $t$ -exact for the perverse $t$ -structure on the left and the standard $t$ -structure on the right. It induces an equivalence of abelian categories

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong\begin{cases}\wedge^{*}(T^{*}\mathbb{A}^{2p})\mathrm{-mod}(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})),&p=q,\\
\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}),&p<q.\end{cases} $$

Here modules and representations are finite-dimensional. The same holds for $\mathfrak{L}X$ with its $\mathfrak{L}^{+}G$ -action.

#### Proof.

Let $\lambda\in\Lambda_{A}^{+}$ be a dominant real coweight, and let $V^{\lambda}\in\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{Sp}_{2p})$ and $\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}}$ be the corresponding irreducible representation and IC complex. It follows from the construction that

$$ \Phi^{b}(\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}})\cong\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}\otimes V^{\lambda},\qquad\kappa(\mathfrak{B}_{p,q}\otimes V^{\lambda})\cong V^{\lambda}. $$

Hence $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}(\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}})\cong V^{\lambda}$ lies in the standard heart. According to Proposition 2.4.4(1), the simple perverse sheaves are the $\mathrm{IC}^{\lambda}_{\mathbf{R}}$ . Since every object of the perverse heart has finite length, $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}$ sends this heart into the standard heart. Both $t$ -structures are bounded, so $\kappa\circ\Phi^{b}$ is $t$ -exact and induces an equivalence

$$ \mathrm{Perv}_{\mathfrak{L}^{+}U(p,q)}(\mathrm{Gr}_{U(p,q)})\cong D^{\mathrm{Sp}_{2p}}_{fd}(\mathfrak{A}_{p,q}\mathrm{-mod})^{\heartsuit}. $$

The theorem follows from the description of the heart above. The assertion for $\mathfrak{L}X$ follows from Proposition 2.4.5. ∎

## 1. Introduction

Throughout this paper we work locally at a prime $p$ . Inspired by the work of Schwänzl-Vogt-Waldhausen in [SVW99], the first author showed:

#### Theorem 1.1 ([Dev20, Theorem 1.3]).

Let $h\geq 1$ and $p^{k}>2$ . Then a $T(h)$ -local11 1 The version of this result for $K(h)$ and $T(h)$ are equivalent by the nilpotence theorem: see [LMMT24, Lemma 2.3]. $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -ring cannot have a primitive $p^{k}$ th root of unity $\zeta_{p^{k}}$ in its $\pi_{0}$ .

This result can be viewed as saying that ramification in the homotopy rings of $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -rings behaves quite differently at heights $\geq 1$ than at height $0$ . Our goal in this note is to understand the extent to which this phenomenon continues for $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -rings for $n<\infty$ .

Given an even $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring $R$ , it is not hard to adjoin roots of unity as an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -ring. Namely, one starts with the polynomial ring $R[x]$ , and use [Ang08, Corollary 3.2] to obtain an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -ring structure on $R[x]/\Phi_{m}(x)$ , where $\Phi_{m}$ is the $m^{\text{th}}$ cyclotomic polynomial. Thus the first $m$ for which there might be obstructions to adding roots of unity to $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -rings is $n=2$ . We show that there are indeed obstructions in this case.

#### Theorem A.

Let $h\geq 1$ . There is a $k\geq 0$ depending on $p,h$ such that a $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring cannot have $\zeta_{p^{k}}$ in $\pi_{0}$ .

We obtain this result as a consequence of the more general result below, which obstructs perfectoid rings from mapping into the $\pi_{0}$ of nonzero $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -rings. Theorem A is a consequence of taking $S$ to be $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ the $p$ -adic completion of the maximal $p$ -cyclotomic extension of the integers:

#### Theorem B.

Let $R$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring with a map $S\to\pi_{0}R$ where $S$ is a perfectoid ring. Then there is a map of $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -rings $S\to R$ . In particular $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ - $S$ -algebra.

Given Theorem A, we can make the following definition:

#### Definition 1.2.

Fix a prime $p$ , a height $h>0$ , and an $n\geq 2$ . The numbers $r_{p,h,n}$ to be the largest natural number such that there exists a $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra with a $p^{r_{p,h,n}}$ -th root of unity in $\pi_{0}$ .

The numbers $r_{p,h,n}$ are nonincreasing in $n$ , and measure the extent to which roots of unity must not exist in $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras. We prove the following results about the numbers $r_{p,h,n}$ :

#### Theorem C.

The following are true about the $r_{p,h,n}$ :

- • $r_{p,1,4}$ is $0$ for $p>2$ and $1$ for $p=2$ .

- • Fix $p$ and $h$ . Then for $n\gg 0$ , $r_{p,h,n}$ is $0$ for $p>2$ and $1$ for $p=2$ .

At height $h=1$ , the above result is proven by using the existence of $\delta$ -operations $\pi_{0}(A)\to\pi_{0}(A/p^{2})$ . In fact, our proof also shows the more general obstruction to ramification in $\mathbf{E}_{4}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebras:

#### Theorem D.

Let $A$ be a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{4}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra. If there is a map from $\mathcal{O}_{K}\to\pi_{0}A$ where $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is the ring of integers of a ramified extension $K$ of $\mathbf{Q}_{p}$ , then $A=0$ .

We also study in Section 3 obstructions to adjoining roots of unity in a strict way, for example showing in Corollary 3.5 that cyclotomic polynomial $\Phi_{p^{k}}(q)$ is not $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -strict in $\mathrm{KU}[q]^{\wedge}_{p}$ for $p^{k}>2$ . This is an obstruction to constructing $\mathrm{KU}[\zeta_{p^{k}}]$ as an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebra in a strict way.

Despite these obstructions, we were suprised to learn that there are $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebras $A$ with a $p$ th root of unity.

#### Example 1.3.

It follows from [Ang08, Theorem 5.17] that there is a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra with $\pi_{0}$ isomorphic to $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p}]$ . This can be obtained from a Hochschild cohomology of a $2$ -periodic form of $K(1)$ . We note [Ang08, Conjecture 5.20] describes an analog of this at higher height.

The above example shows that the number $r_{p,h,n}$ are interesting, and we believe it would be interesting to compute them.

#### Remark 1.4.

One can attempt to study analogues of the statements discussed here for higher roots of unity in the sense of [CSY24, Definition 4.2]. In this case, recall that a primitive $p^{r}$ th root of unity of height $n$ for some $r\geq 1$ in an commutative algebra $R$ in a presentably symmetric monoidal stable category is an $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -map $\mathbbm{1}[B^{n}\mathbf{Z}/p^{r}]\to R$ such that the pushout of commutative algebras of the span $\mathbbm{1}[B^{n}\mathbf{Z}/p^{r-1}]\leftarrow\mathbbm{1}[B^{n}\mathbf{Z}/p^{r}]\to R$ is $0$ .

We then claim that higher primitive roots of unity don’t exist at the wrong height, i.e., if $R$ is a $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra with $h\neq n$ and a primitive $p^{r}$ th root of unity, then $R=0$ . If $n>h$ , then $B^{n}\mathbf{Z}/p^{r}$ is $T(h)$ -acyclic, so the pushout is $R$ itself. If $n<h$ , then because the $T(n)$ -local category is virtually $(\mathbf{F}_{p},n)$ -orientable [BCSY24, Proposition 7.27], we can add a height $n$ $p^{r}$ th root of unity, we can identify this pushout with its Fourier dual [BCSY24, Theorem 7.33], which is $\mathbbm{1}^{B^{h-n}((\mathbf{Z}/p^{r-1})^{\vee})}\leftarrow\mathbbm{1}^{B^{h-n}((\mathbf{Z}/p^{r})^{\vee})}\to R$ . However, for $h-n\geq 1$ , tensoring along the map $\mathbbm{1}^{B^{h-n}((\mathbf{Z}/p^{r})^{\vee}))}\to\mathbbm{1}^{B^{h-n}((\mathbf{Z}/p^{r-1})^{\vee})}$ is conservative, since the target ring has a $B^{h-n-1}(\mathbf{Z}/p)$ -action whose fixed points is the source, and fixed points commutes with colimits by $\infty$ -semiadditivity [CSY22].

We note that the notion of higher primitive roots of unity considered here is much stronger than what is considered in this paper, it is defined for $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -algebras and is a strict notion (see Section 3). It would be interesting to explore the extent to which this phenomenon persists for weaker notions of higher roots of unity.

## 2. Perfectoid rings in $\pi_{0}$

In this section, we prove our main result:

#### Theorem B.

Let $R$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring with a map $S\to\pi_{0}R$ where $S$ is a perfectoid ring. Then there is a map of $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -rings $S\to R$ . In particular, $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ - $S$ -algebra.

As a consequence, we deduce Theorem A.

#### Proof of Theorem A.

Suppose that the conclusion of Theorem A is false. Then for each $k\geq 0$ , there exists a $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring $R_{k}$ such that $\pi_{0}R_{k}$ contains a primitive $p^{k}$ th root of unity $\zeta_{p^{k}}$ . Let $R$ be an ultraproduct of the $R_{k}$ . Then $R$ has nonzero $T(h)$ -localization: this is because it is a filtered colimit of non-zero $T(h)$ -local rings given by products of the $R_{k}$ , and $T(h)$ -local filtered colimits of nonzero $T(h)$ -local rings are nonzero (see the proof of [BSY26, Lemma A.11]). But $\pi_{0}(R)$ contains a system of primitive $p$ th roots of unity, so there is a map $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}\to\pi_{0}(R)$ . Applying Theorem B to the perfectoid ring $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ , we obtain a contradiction, since $\mathbf{Z}_{p}^{\mathrm{cyc}}$ is $T(h)$ -acyclic. ∎

We now turn to proving Theorem B. Recall that there is a spherical Witt vector functor $\mathbb{W}:\mathrm{Perf}_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}\to\mathrm{CAlg}(\mathrm{Sp}_{p})$ . To prove Theorem B, we first show that $R$ lifts to an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebra over $\mathbb{W}((S/p)^{\flat})$ , which follows from the fact that spherical Witt vectors always act centrally on $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras (Proposition 2.2 below). Then we conclude by applying a perfectoid version of the Hopkins–Mahowald theorem due to Mao (Proposition 2.4), which implies that the existence of an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -map from $S$ to an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathbb{W}((S/p)^{\flat})$ -algebra can be checked on $\pi_{0}$ .

We begin with the proposition below, which is an analogue of [BSY26, Proposition 2.2] in the setting of $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras.

#### Proposition 2.1.

For $n\geq 2$ , the composite $\mathbb{W}:\mathrm{Perf}_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}\to\mathrm{CAlg}(\mathrm{Sp}_{p})\to\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}(\mathrm{Sp}_{p})$ is fully faithful with right adjoint $(-)^{\flat}$ , sending $R$ to $(\pi_{0}R/p)^{\flat}$ .

#### Proof.

We first show that for $n\geq 2$ , $\mathbb{W}(A)$ is formally étale as a $p$ -complete $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra, i.e that the $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -cotangent complex vanishes. To do this, it suffices by [Fra13, Theorem 2.26, Proposition 3.16] to show that $\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}-0}\mathbb{W}(A)\cong\mathbb{W}(A)$ . Because $\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n}-0}\mathbb{W}(A)\cong\mathbb{W}(A)\otimes_{\int_{\mathbf{R}^{n-1}-0}\mathbb{W}(A)}\mathbb{W}(A)$ , it suffices to show this for $n=2$ , and since $\mathbb{W}$ is symmetric monoidal, it suffices to show this in $\mathrm{Perf}_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}$ for $A$ . This follows since

$$ \int_{\mathbf{R}^{2}-0}A\cong A\otimes_{A\otimes A}A\cong A $$

It follows from the existence of the adjunction that $\mathbb{W}(A)$ is fully faithful, so it only remains to show the adjunction, i.e produce a natural isomorphism

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}(\mathrm{Sp}_{p})}(\mathbb{W}(A),R)\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Perf}_{\mathbf{F}_{p}}}(A,(\pi_{0}R/p)^{\flat}) $$

To do this, since $\mathbb{W}(A)$ is connective, it suffices to assume that $R$ is connective. Then since the Postnikov tower of $R$ is a tower of square zero extensions and $\mathbb{W}(A)$ is formally étale, we reduce to the case $R$ is discrete, where the result is now clear, since $\pi_{0}\mathbb{W}(A)\cong\mathrm{W}(A)$ . ∎

The next key observation in proving Theorem B is that the counit map $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to R$ is always central. Recall from [Lur16, Section 5.3] and [Fra13, Definition 3.1, Proposition 3.16] that the $\mathbf{E}_{n+1}$ -center of an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra $R$ is given by the endomorphism algebra $\End_{\int_{S^{n-1}\times\mathbf{R}}R}(R)$ .

#### Proposition 2.2.

Given a $p$ -complete $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra $R$ with $n\geq 2$ , $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ - $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})$ -algebra. Moreover, $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}(R)^{\flat}\cong R^{\flat}$ , where $\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{n}}(R)$ is the $\mathbf{E}_{n+1}$ center of $R$ .

#### Proof.

First we refine the $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra map $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to R$ to an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra map $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ . To do this, it suffices by the universal property of $\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ ([Lur16, Definition 5.3.1.2]) to produce a diagram of $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras

To do this, we consider the base-change along the multiplication map, which a priori is a map of $\mathbf{E}_{n-1}$ -algebras:

$$ m:\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\otimes R\to(\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\otimes R)\otimes_{\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat}\otimes R^{\flat})}\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat}). $$

Next, we note that the target of $m$ is an idempotent algebra over the source: this follows because $\mathbb{W}$ takes surjective maps to idempotent algebras, and we are basechanging along such a map. Thus $m$ canonically refines to an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra map. Because $1\otimes R$ can be written as an $\mathbf{E}_{n-1}$ -algebra map as $R\to R\otimes_{\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})}\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat}\otimes R^{\flat})$ via the right unit, we find that $m\circ(1\otimes R)$ is an equivalence22 2 A subtlety is that it apriori is only the identity map as an $\mathbf{E}_{n-1}$ -ring map. But any equivalence is equivalent to the identity map, so this doesn’t matter.. This gives the desired triangle.

Since we have an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra map $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ , by applying Proposition 2.1 it follows that the map $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ automatically refines to an $\mathbf{E}_{n+1}$ -map, since the mapping spaces in $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ and $\mathbf{E}_{n+1}$ -algebras are the same. Since $R$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ - $\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ -algebra, it follows that it is also an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ - $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})$ -algebra.

To finish, we now show that $\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)^{\flat}\to R^{\flat}$ is an isomorphism. Surjectivity follows from the lift $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})\to\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)$ we have already produced. For injectivity, if $a$ is in the kernel, then we consider the map of $\mathbf{E}_{n+1}$ -algebras $g:\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)\to\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)\otimes_{\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p}[x]^{\sharp})}\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ where $x$ is sent to $a$ . Here $\sharp$ denotes the colimit perfection. Since $\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is an idempotent algebra over $\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p}[x]^{\sharp})$ , the target is an idempotent algebra over the source. Since $a$ is in the kernel, we learn that $R^{\flat}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ - $\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)\otimes_{\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p}[x]^{\sharp})}\mathbb{W}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ -algebra, so that $g$ has a section via the universal property of the center. It follows that $a=0$ . ∎

#### Remark 2.3.

The lift of $R$ to an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ - $\mathbb{W}(R^{\flat})$ -algebra is essentially unique. Indeed, the space $L$ of lifts is the pullback

which is contractible since the right vertical map is an isomorphism as $\mathfrak{Z}_{n}(R)^{\flat}\cong R^{\flat}$ .

The last ingredient for Theorem B is the perfectoid version of the Hopkins–Mahowald theorem, which we now explain. Let $S$ be a perfectoid ring. Then the map $\mathrm{W}(S^{\flat})\to S$ on $\pi_{0}$ is Fontaine’s map $\theta:A_{\mathrm{inf}}(S)\to S$ . The kernel of $\theta$ is a principal ideal, with a generator $\xi$ , giving $S=A_{\mathrm{inf}}(S)/\xi$ as discrete rings. This has the following lift to $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -spectral algebraic geometry:

#### Proposition 2.4 ([Mao23, Theorem 1.13]).

Let $S$ be a perfectoid ring. Then there is an isomorphism of $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebras $\mathbb{W}(S^{\flat})\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{2}}\xi\cong S$ , where $\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{2}}$ is the $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -quotient, i.e., the free $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathbb{W}(S^{\flat})$ -algebra equipped with a nullhomotopy of $\xi$ .

For $S=\mathbf{F}_{p}$ , this is the Hopkins–Mahowald theorem [ACB19, Theorem 5.1].

#### Proof of Theorem B.

Because we have a map $\pi_{0}S\to\pi_{0}R$ , we have a map $\mathbb{W}(S)\to\mathbb{W}(R)$ , making $R$ an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathbb{W}(S)$ -algebra. Since $d$ is sent to $0$ in $R$ , Proposition 2.4 produces an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebra map $S\to R$ . ∎

## 3. Strict elements

We now show that there are strong restrictions on $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras with strict roots of unity for $n>1$ . We first define the notion of an $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -strict element of an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra, which is inductive on $m-n$ .

#### Definition 3.1.

Let $R$ be an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra, $x\in\pi_{0}R$ , and $m\in\mathbf{N}\cup\infty$ . We say $x$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -strict element if

- • If $m\leq n$ , we ask for the existence of an $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -algebra map $\mathbb{S}[t]\to R$ sending the generator $t$ to $x$ .

- • If $n<m<\infty$ , we ask that $x$ lift to an $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -strict element of $\pi_{0}\mathfrak{Z}_{n}R$ .

- • If $m=\infty$ , we ask for $x$ to be $\mathbf{E}_{k}$ -strict for all $k<\infty$ compatibly in $k$ .

For example, Proposition 2.2 can be interpreted as saying that when $x$ lifts to $\mathrm{W}(R^{\flat})$ , it is $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -strict. If $x$ is $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -strict, then so are all of the powers of $x$ (including negative powers, if they exist). There is also a variation of the notion of $\mathbf{E}_{m}$ -strict, where for an operad $\mathcal{O}\to\mathbf{E}_{n}$ , we say that an element $x$ in $\pi_{0}$ of an $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebra $R$ is $\mathcal{O}$ -strict if there is an $\mathcal{O}$ -algebra map $\mathbb{S}[t]\to R$ sending the generator $t$ to $x$ .

#### Proposition 3.2.

Suppose that $p^{k}\neq 1,2$ . Let $R$ be a $p$ -complete $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring with a primitive $p^{k}$ th root of unity $\zeta_{p^{k}}$ which is $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -strict. Then $R$ admits an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -map from $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p^{k}}]$ , and in particular is an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ - $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p^{k}}]$ -algebra.

#### Proof.

Since $\zeta_{p^{k}}$ is an $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -strict element, there is an $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -map $\mathbb{S}[q]\to\mathfrak{Z}_{\mathbf{E}_{2}}R$ which makes $R$ into an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathbb{S}[q]$ -algebra. The claim follows once we show that the free $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ - $\mathbb{S}_{p}[q]$ -algebra with $q$ a root of unity in $\pi_{0}$ is $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p^{k}}]$ . This is [Mao23, Theorem 1.19], but we quickly recall the argument for completeness. There is an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -map $\mathbb{S}_{p}[q]\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{2}}\Phi_{p^{k}}(q)\to\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p^{n+1}}]$ . Both target and source are complete with respect to $q-1$ , so it suffices to check that this map is an equivalence after base-changing along the map $\mathbb{S}_{p}[q]\to\mathbb{S}_{p}$ sending $q\mapsto 1$ . After base-change, this becomes the map $\mathbb{S}_{p}\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{2}}p\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ , which is an equivalence by the Hopkins–Mahowald theorem. ∎

If $R$ is an even $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -algebra, there are no obstructions to any $x\in\pi_{0}R$ being $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -strict, since the cells of $\mathbb{S}[t]$ as an $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -ring are in even degrees. As a consequence we can adjoin any algebraic equation33 3 One can also add multiple generators and relations at the same time. $R[x]/(f)$ as a basechange $R[x]\otimes_{\mathbb{S}_{p}[f]}\mathbb{S}$ , in particular allowing us to add roots of unity as an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -algebra (see also [Ang08, Theorem 3.1]).

Our next goal is to show using the Rezk logarithm [Rez06] that when $R$ is a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -ring, any unit which is $\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -strict (for example an $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -strict element) is $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -strict. Recall that the $\pi_{0}$ of $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -rings naturally admits the structure of a $\delta$ -ring, with lift of Frobenius $\psi(x)=x^{p}+p\delta(x)$ , and that $L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}$ is the free polynomial algebra on $\delta^{i}(t)$ for $i\geq 0$ [Hop14].

We first record a well known lemma. Let $\mathbb{S}\{t\}$ denote the free $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -ring on a class $t$ in degree $0$ .

#### Lemma 3.3.

There is an equivalence of $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -rings $L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}[t]\cong L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}\delta(t)$ . Here, the quotient on the right-hand side is taken in $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -rings.

#### Proof.

Since $\delta(t)=0$ in $L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}[t]$ , there is an $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -map $L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}\delta(t)\to L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}[t]$ . To see this is an equivalence, McClure’s theorem [BMMS86, Chapter IX] (see also [Hop14]) shows that $\pi_{*}L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}$ is a $p$ -completed polynomial ring over $\pi_{*}L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}$ on $\delta^{i}(t)$ for $i\geq 0$ . Since $L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}\sslash_{\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}\delta(t)\cong L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{t\}\hat{\otimes}_{L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}\{\delta(t)\}}L_{K(1)}\mathbb{S}$ , it follows from the $p$ -completed bar spectral sequence that the map is an equivalence. ∎

#### Proposition 3.4.

Let $A$ be a $K(1)$ -local ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{KU}_{p}$ -algebra with $\pi_{0}(A)$ torsion free, and let $\xi\in\pi_{0}(A)^{\times}$ . If $\xi$ is $\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -strict, then it is $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -strict. In particular, $\delta(\xi)=0$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 3.3, it suffices to show that $\delta(\xi)=0$ if $\xi$ is $\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -strict. We begin by observing that

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{1}}(\mathrm{Sp})}(\mathbb{S}[t],A)\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}}(\mathcal{S})}(\mathbf{N},\Omega^{\infty}A) $$

where the target has the $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ structure coming from multiplication. Since $\xi$ is in a unit, using $(-)_{\xi}$ to denote the component sending $1$ to $\xi$ , we get

$$ \mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{1}}(\mathrm{Sp})}(\mathbb{S}[t],A)_{\xi}\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}}(\mathcal{S})}(\mathbf{Z},\mathrm{GL}_{1}A)_{\xi}\cong\mathrm{Map}_{\mathrm{Alg}_{\mathbf{A}_{2}}(\mathcal{S})}(B^{2}\mathbf{Z},B^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A))_{\xi} $$

In other words, we need to show that given a commutative diagram of the form

$$ \textstyle{{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty}\times{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu} \scriptstyle{\xi,\xi} \textstyle{\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\times\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\xi} \textstyle{\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A).} $$

$\delta(\xi)=0$ .

To understand this, we will use the $K(1)$ -local logarithm, which defines an infinite loop map $\ell:\mathrm{B}^{2}\mathrm{GL}_{1}(A)\to\Omega^{\infty}\Sigma^{2}A$ since $A$ is $K(1)$ -local. After composing with the logarithm, we obtain a diagram

$$ \textstyle{\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}({\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty}\times{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty})\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\mu} \scriptstyle{\ell(\xi),\ell(\xi)} \textstyle{\Sigma^{2}(A\oplus A)\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sim} \textstyle{A\oplus A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \textstyle{\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty}\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\ell(\xi)} \textstyle{\Sigma^{2}A\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces\ignorespaces} \scriptstyle{\sim} \textstyle{A.} $$

The final column uses multiplication by $\beta$ to identify $\Sigma^{2}A\simeq A$ . Since $A$ is complex orientable and $2$ -periodic, a choice of orientation and periodicity generator gives an isomorphism $[\Sigma^{\infty}_{+}{\mathbf{CP}}^{\infty},L_{K(1)}A]\cong\pi_{0}L_{K(1)}A[\![x]\!]$ , to which $\ell(\xi)$ corresponds to a power series $f$ . The commutativity of the diagram implies that $f$ is a homomorphism from the formal group of $A$ to the additive formal group.

Over a torsion free ring, up to rescaling the Lie algebra, there is a unique homomorphism between any two formal groups, which to the additive formal group is given by the logarithm. In the case of $A$ , which is a $\mathrm{KU}_{p}$ -algebra, this is given by $f(x)=a\sum_{n\geq 1}\frac{x^{n}}{n}$ . Since $\pi_{0}A$ is $p$ -torsion free, and $A$ is $p$ -complete, $\pi_{0}A$ is $p$ -adically separated, so $a=0$ for $f$ to be an integral power series, i.e $\ell(\xi)=0$ .

By [Rez06, Theorem 1.9], we have

$$ 0=\ell(\xi)=\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n}\frac{p^{n-1}}{n}\left(\frac{\delta(\xi)}{\xi^{p}}\right)^{n}=\frac{1}{p}\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{\xi^{p}}{\psi(\xi)}\right). $$

Using that $p\in\pi_{0}(A)$ has divided powers, we can multiply by $p$ and exponentiate to get

$$ 1=\exp\left(p\ell(\xi)\right)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\ell(\xi)^{n}\frac{p^{n}}{n!}=\frac{\xi^{p}}{\psi(\xi)} $$

Thus $\psi(\xi)=\xi^{p}+p\delta(\xi)=\xi^{p}$ so $\delta(\xi)=0$ . ∎

As discussed earlier, we can adjoin primitive $p^{k}$ th roots of unity to even algebras (such as $\mathrm{KU}$ ) as an $\mathbf{E}_{1}$ -ring by using the fact that the element $\Phi_{p^{k}}(q)$ is $\mathbf{E}_{2}$ -strict in $\mathrm{KU}[q]$ . The following corollary shows that this method cannot be improved even to get an $\mathbf{E}_{1}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -structure, and nor can any other similar kind of strict quotient.

#### Corollary 3.5.

The element $\Phi_{p^{k}}(q)$ is not $\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -strict in $\mathrm{KU}[q]^{\wedge}_{p}$ if $p^{k}\neq 1,2$ .

#### Proof.

If $\Phi_{p^{k}}(q)$ were $\mathbf{E}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{A}_{2}$ -strict, it would be $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -strict by Proposition 3.4. But then the tensor product $\mathbb{S}\otimes_{\mathbb{S}[t]}\mathrm{KU}[q]^{\wedge}_{p}$ would be a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -ring having a primitive $p^{k}$ th root of unity in $\pi_{0}$ , contradicting Theorem 1.1. ∎

## 4. $K(1)$ -local ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebras

The goal of this section is to prove Theorem C. The key point is Proposition 4.2 below, that $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2n+2}$ -algebras have a lift of Frobenius mod $p^{n}$ . This makes the obstruction to roots of unity from Theorem 1.1 still hold, and it moreover generalizes to more general ramified extensions. We then use an ultraproduct argument to show that $r_{p,h,n}$ agrees with the number for $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ for $n$ sufficiently large.

#### Proposition 4.1.

There is a square as below, where the vertical maps are isomorphisms, and the lower horizontal map is the $p^{n}$ -Bockstein:

#### Proof.

For $p>2$ , this follows from the commutative diagram on [BHK24, Section 6.2, Page 44]. For $p=2$ , note that $\mathrm{Conf}_{2}(\mathbf{R}^{2n+1})\cong\mathbf{RP}^{2n}$ , and the map to $B\Sigma_{2}=\mathbf{RP}^{\infty}$ is the standard inclusion. Upon $2$ -completion, both $\mathrm{KU}\otimes\mathbf{RP}^{2n}$ and $\mathrm{KU}\otimes\mathbf{RP}^{\infty}$ are perfect $\mathrm{KU}_{2}$ -modules, so it suffices to identify the $\mathrm{KU}_{2}$ -linear dual of the map $\mathrm{KU}_{2}\otimes\mathbf{RP}^{2n}\to(\mathrm{KU}\otimes\mathbf{RP}^{\infty})_{2}$ with the map $\mathrm{KU}_{2}\to\mathrm{KU}/2^{n}$ . This follows from [Pow15, Corollary 4.17]. ∎

Below, we use the map $p:X/p^{n}\to X/p^{n+1}$ for a spectrum $X$ .

#### Proposition 4.2.

Suppose that $R$ is a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2n+2}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra. Then there is a natural map

$$ \delta:\pi_{0}R\to\pi_{0}(R/p^{n}) $$

such that

$$ \displaystyle\delta(x+y) \displaystyle=\delta(x)+\delta(y)-\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{p}{i}}{p}x^{i}y^{p-i}, \displaystyle\delta(xy) \displaystyle=\delta(x)y^{p}+\delta(y)x^{p}+p\delta(x)\delta(y). $$

In particular, the map $\phi:\pi_{0}R\to\pi_{0}(R/p^{n+1})$ defined by $\phi(x)=x^{p}+p\delta(x)$ , is a ring homomorphism lifting the Frobenius map.

#### Proof.

We will define the map $\delta$ for all $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{2n+1}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebras, and show that it satisfies the desired relations for all $\mathbf{E}_{2n+2}$ -algebras.

To define the map $\delta$ , it suffices to do this in the universal example of the free $\mathbf{E}_{2n+1}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra on a class $x$ in degree $0$ . From Proposition 4.1, we learn that in arity $p$ , the map from the free $\mathbf{E}_{2n+1}$ -algebra to the free $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra is an isomorphism on $\pi_{0}/p^{n}$ , allowing us to define $\delta$ as the unique lift of the associated $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -operation.

For the relations, it suffices to prove them in the universal $\mathbf{E}_{2n+2}$ -algebra on two classes in degree $0$ . The relation for $\delta(x+y)$ is witnessed in the arity $p$ part of this free algebra, which is $((\mathrm{KU}\oplus\mathrm{KU})^{\otimes p}\otimes(\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{2n+2}))_{+}))_{h\Sigma_{p}}$ . We claim that the map

$$ ((\mathrm{KU}\oplus\mathrm{KU})^{\otimes p}\otimes(\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{2n+2}))_{+}))_{h\Sigma_{p}}/p^{n}\to((\mathrm{KU}\oplus\mathrm{KU})^{\otimes p}_{h\Sigma_{p}}/p^{n} $$

is injective on the image of $\pi_{0}((\mathrm{KU}\oplus\mathrm{KU})^{\otimes p}\otimes(\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{2n+1}))_{+}))_{h\Sigma_{p}}/p^{n}$ in $\pi_{0}$ . The result then follows, since the target is the arity $p$ part of the universal $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra on two generators, where the desired relation holds.

To see the claim, we note that ( $p$ -adically), $((\mathrm{KU}\oplus\mathrm{KU})^{\otimes p}\otimes(\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{i}))_{+}))_{h\Sigma_{p}}$ naturally is a sum of two copies of $\mathrm{KU}^{\otimes p}\otimes\mathrm{Conf}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{i})_{h\Sigma_{p}}$ , and a sum of copies of $\mathrm{Conf}_{p}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathbf{R}^{i})_{+}$ indexed by the nontrivial $\Sigma_{p}$ orbits of $2^{p}$ . The claim then follows from the fact that the inclusion $\mathrm{Conf}_{p}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathbf{R}^{i})\to\mathrm{Conf}_{p}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathbf{R}^{i+1})$ is null, so the image factors through a section from $\mathrm{Conf}_{p}^{\mathrm{ord}}(\mathbf{R}^{\infty})$ .

The proof of the relation for $\delta(xy)$ is nearly identical, except the relation takes place in arity $2p$ instead of $p$ .

Once these relations are proven, it follows that $\varphi$ is a ring map and a lift of Frobenius, for the same reason that a delta structure gives a lift of Frobenius. ∎

#### Remark 4.3.

The relations satisfied by $\delta$ are different if $R$ is only an $\mathbf{E}_{2n+1}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra, and can involve Browder brackets.

We sketch how this works for the relation $\delta(xy)=\delta(x)y^{2}+\delta(y)x^{2}+2\delta(x)\delta(y)$ for $p=2$ and $n=1$ . In this case, $\beta\delta$ lifts to a natural map $\pi_{0}(R)\to\pi_{2}(R/2)$ for an $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ - $\mathrm{ku}$ -algebra. Moreover, mod $\beta$ , it is easy to see that this operation is the Dyer–Lashof operation $Q_{2}$ on $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ - $\mathbf{F}_{2}$ -algebras. The nontriviality of the Browder bracket term then follows from the fact that the Cartan formula for $Q_{2}$ of an $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ -algebra has a Browder bracket term: it is given by $Q_{2}(xy)=Q_{2}(x)y^{2}+x^{2}Q_{2}(y)+x[x,y]y$ (see [Law19, Theorem 5.2]), using that $Q_{1}$ vanishes since the classes $x,y$ are integral.

It is possible that arguments similar to ours are able to prove the analog of Theorem D for $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{3}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebras, and we believe it would be interesting to work this out.

Using Proposition 4.2, we can prove Theorem D, which is the key input to Theorem C.

#### Theorem D.

Let $A$ be a $K(1)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{4}$ - $\mathrm{KU}$ -algebra. If there is a map from $\mathcal{O}_{K}\to\pi_{0}A$ where $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ is the ring of integers of a ramified extension $K$ of $\mathbf{Q}_{p}$ , then $A=0$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\pi$ be a uniformizer of $\mathcal{O}_{K}$ , with valuation $\frac{1}{e}$ where $e>1$ by assumption. Let $a$ be an integer minimally chosen so that $\frac{ap}{e}\geq 1$ . Note that $a<e$ . Then $\varphi(\pi^{a})\equiv\pi^{ap}\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ . On the other hand, $\varphi(\pi^{e})|\varphi(p)=p$ . It follows that $p\varphi(\pi^{e-a})|\varphi(\pi^{e})|p$ . But $\varphi(\pi^{e-a})$ is nilpotent in $\pi_{0}(A/p^{2})$ , so we learn that $p=0$ in $\pi_{0}(A/p^{2})$ , and hence also in the subring $\pi_{0}(A)/p^{2}$ . This means that $p=p^{2}x$ for some $x\in\pi_{0}(A)$ . Applying $\delta$ , we obtain that $\delta(p)=\delta(p^{2}x)$ in $\pi_{0}(A/p)$ . However $\delta(p^{2}x)$ is divisible by $p$ and $\delta(p)$ is a unit, so we learn that $A/p=0$ , and hence $A=0$ . ∎

#### Proof of Theorem C.

The fact that $r_{p,1,4}=0$ for $p>2$ and $r_{2,1,4}=1$ follows from Theorem D since $\mathbf{Z}_{p}[\zeta_{p}]$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{2}[\zeta_{4}]$ come from ramified extensions of $\mathbf{Q}_{p}$ and $\mathbf{Q}_{2}$ respectively.

We now show that if we fix $p$ and $h$ , then for $n\gg 0$ , the number $r_{p,h,n}$ is $0$ if $p>2$ and is $1$ if $p=2$ . If this were false, then there woud be a sequence $R_{n}$ of nonzero $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{n}$ -algebras containing a $p^{\text{th}}$ (resp. $4^{\text{th}}$ for $p=2$ ) root of unity. The ultraproduct of these would then be a nonzero $T(h)$ -local $\mathbf{E}_{\infty}$ -algebra with such a root of unity, contradicting Theorem 1.1. ∎

# Lifting to truncated Brown-Peterson spectra and Hodge-de Rham degeneration in characteristic $p>0$ Thanks: Part of this work was done when the author was supported by the PD Soros Fellowship and NSF DGE-2140743. I’m grateful to Ben Antieau, Bhargav Bhatt, Jeremy Hahn, and the referee for suggestions which improved this note.

**Authors:** S. K. Devalapurkar Address: 1 Oxford St, Cambridge, MA 02139 Email address: sdevalapurkar@math.harvard.edu, August 24, 2026

## Abstract

The goal of this note is to prove that Hodge-de Rham degeneration holds for smooth and proper $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -schemes $X$ with $\dim(X)<p^{n}$ assuming that two conditions hold: its category of quasicoherent sheaves admits a lift to the truncated Brown-Peterson spectrum $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ ; and the Hochschild-Kostant-Rosenberg spectral sequence for $X$ degenerates at the $E_{2}$ -page. This result is obtained from a noncommutative version thereof, whose proof is essentially the same as Mathew’s argument in [Mat20].

Let $X$ be a smooth and proper scheme over a perfect field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ . In [DI87], Deligne and Illusie proved that the Hodge decomposition holds for the de Rham cohomology of $X$ under certain hypotheses: namely, if $\dim(X)<p$ and $X$ admits a smooth and proper lift to the truncated Witt vectors $W_{2}(k)=W(k)/p^{2}$ , they showed that the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence

$$ E_{1}^{\ast,\ast}=\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\Omega^{\ast}_{X/k})\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k) $$

collapses at the $E_{1}$ -page.

In [DI87, Remarque 2.6(iii)] (see also [Ill96, Problem 7.10]), Deligne and Illusie asked if the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence could degenerate for a smooth proper $k$ -scheme $X$ with a lift to $W(k)/p^{2}$ (or even to $W(k)$ ), without any dimension assumptions. This remarkable question has recently been answered (in the negative) by Sasha Petrov in [Pet23]. Our goal in this note is to study conditions on $X$ arising from chromatic homotopy theory which do guarantee Hodge-de Rham degeneration if $\dim(X)>p$ .

#### Recollection 1.

Let $X$ be a smooth scheme over a commutative ring $k$ . One then has the HKR and de-Rham-to- $\mathrm{HP}$ spectral sequences (see [ABM21, Definition 3.1]):

$$ \displaystyle E_{2}^{s,t}=\mathrm{H}^{s}(X;\wedge^{-t}L_{X/k}) \displaystyle\Rightarrow\pi_{-(s+t)}\mathrm{HH}(X/k), \displaystyle E_{2}^{s,t}=\mathrm{H}^{s-t}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k) \displaystyle\Rightarrow\pi_{-(s+t)}\mathrm{HP}(X/k). $$

There are also the Hodge-de Rham and the Tate spectral sequences

$$ \displaystyle E_{1}^{s,t}=\mathrm{H}^{s}(X;\wedge^{t}L_{X/k}) \displaystyle\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{s+t}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/k), \displaystyle E_{2}^{s,t}=\hat{\mathrm{H}}^{s}(BS^{1};\pi_{t}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p})) \displaystyle\Rightarrow\pi_{t-s}\mathrm{HP}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p}), $$

where $\hat{\mathrm{H}}$ denotes Tate cohomology. Note that if we write $\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(BS^{1};\mathbf{F}_{p})=\mathbf{F}_{p}[\hbar]$ with $\hbar$ in cohomological degree $2$ , then the $E_{2}$ -page of the Tate spectral sequence can be rewritten as $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p})[\hbar^{\pm 1}]$ .

Let $n\leq\infty$ . Fix an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -form of the ( $p$ -completed) truncated Brown-Peterson spectrum $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ of height $n-1$ , which exists thanks to [HW20, Theorem A]. By construction, $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle\cong\mathbf{Z}_{p}[v_{1},\cdots,v_{n-1}]$ for classes $v_{i}$ in degree $2p^{i}-2$ . By convention, $\mathrm{BP}\langle{-1}\rangle=\mathbf{F}_{p}$ . We also have $\mathrm{BP}\langle{0}\rangle=\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ , and $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle$ can be identified with the connective cover of the Adams summand of $p$ -completed complex K-theory. There is also a tight relationship between $\mathrm{BP}\langle{2}\rangle$ and elliptic cohomology. When $n=\infty$ , the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -ring $\mathrm{BP}\langle{\infty}\rangle$ is denoted $\mathrm{BP}$ , and is called the Brown-Peterson spectrum.

Our goal in this note is to prove:

#### Theorem 2.

Let $n\leq\infty$ , and let $X$ be a smooth and proper scheme over11 1 Here, $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ could be replaced by any perfect field of characteristic $p>0$ ; we only use $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ to avoid introducing conceptually unnecessary notation. $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ of dimension $<p^{n}$ . Suppose that:

- (a) The HKR spectral sequence degenerates at the $E_{2}$ -page; and

- (b) $\QCoh(X)$ lifts to a smooth and proper left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category22 2 Recall that at the beginning of this article, we picked an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -form of $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ , which exists by [HW20, Theorem A]. Then, a “left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category” is simply a left $\mathrm{LMod}_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}$ -module in $\mathrm{Pr^{L}}$ , where $\mathrm{LMod}_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}$ is equipped with the ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -monoidal structure arising from the ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -structure on $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ . See [Lur17, Variant D.1.5.1]..

Then the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence

$$ E_{1}^{\ast,\ast}=\mathrm{H}^{\ast}(X;\Omega^{\ast}_{X/\mathbf{F}_{p}})\Rightarrow\mathrm{H}^{\ast}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X/\mathbf{F}_{p}) $$

collapses at the $E_{1}$ -page, and the de-Rham-to- $\mathrm{HP}$ spectral sequence collapses at the $E_{2}$ -page.

The discussion in [ABM21, Remark 3.6] implies that if the HKR and Tate spectral sequences both degenerate, then both the Hodge-de Rham and de Rham-to- $\mathrm{HP}$ spectral sequences must also degenerate. It therefore suffices to prove the following noncommutative statement33 3 Our original proof used the higher chromatic topological Sen operators from our forthcoming article [Dev23] to argue in a manner similar to [BL22a, Example 4.7.17], but we soon realized that the argument could be simplified much further. In [Dev23, Remark C.14], we also phrase an analogue of Proposition 3 in stacky language via the Sen operator of [BL22a] and the stack $BW^{\times}[F^{n}]$ . The expected isomorphism, which we hope to study in joint work with Jeremy Hahn and Arpon Raksit, between $BW^{\times}[F^{n}]$ and the stack associated to the motivic filtration of $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)^{t{\mathbf{Z}/p}}/(p,\cdots,v_{n-1})$ was the original motivation for our result.:

#### Proposition 3.

Let $n\leq\infty$ , and let $\mathcal{C}$ be a smooth and proper $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -linear $\infty$ -category such that $\pi_{j}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p})=0$ for $j\not\in[-p^{n},p^{n}]$ . If $\mathcal{C}$ lifts to a smooth and proper left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category, then the Tate spectral sequence

$$ E_{2}^{\ast,\ast}=\hat{\mathrm{H}}^{\ast}(BS^{1};\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p}))\Rightarrow\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{HP}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p}) $$

collapses at the $E_{2}$ -page.

#### Remark 4.

When $n=1$ , Theorem 2 is part of the main result of [DI87]44 4 As the reader may have noticed, the title of this work is a tribute to the inspirational paper [DI87].: in this case, condition (b) in Theorem 2 is asking for a lifting to $\mathrm{BP}\langle{0}\rangle=\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ . As mentioned above, Sasha Petrov recently constructed in [Pet23] a $(p+1)$ -dimensional smooth and proper $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ -scheme $\mathfrak{X}$ such that the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence for its special fiber $\mathfrak{X}_{p=0}$ does not degenerate at the $E_{1}$ -page. If the HKR spectral sequence degenerates at the $E_{2}$ -page for Petrov’s $\mathfrak{X}_{p=0}$ , then $\QCoh(\mathfrak{X})$ provides an example of a $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ -linear $\infty$ -category which cannot lift to a $\mathrm{ku}$ -linear $\infty$ -category.

We view Theorem 2 as a step towards a positive answer of Deligne and Illusie’s question in some generality. Note that condition (b) in Theorem 2 is significantly weaker than asking that $X$ itself admit some sort of lifting as a spectral scheme. Note, also, that we do not prove anything nearly as refined as [DI87]: namely, we do not provide any sort of correspondence between liftings and splittings of truncations of the de Rham complex. For instance, it would be very interesting if, for a $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ -scheme $\mathfrak{X}$ , there were a relationship between splittings of the mod $p$ reduction $\widehat{\Omega}^{\not{D}}_{\mathfrak{X},0}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}_{p}}\mathbf{F}_{p}$ of the zeroth generalized eigenspace of the diffracted Hodge complex (see [BL22a, Remark 4.7.20] for this notion) and liftings of $\QCoh(\mathfrak{X})$ to $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle$ .

#### Remark 5.

Let $I=(p^{2},v_{1}^{2},\cdots,v_{n-1}^{2})$ . Were $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle/I$ to admit the structure of an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -ring, Theorem 2 (and Proposition 3) would continue to hold with $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ replaced by $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle/I$ . This is because one can prove that Lemma 10 continues to hold for $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle/I$ .

Some preliminary calculations seem to suggest that Petrov’s first Sen class (see [Pet23, Ill22]) is related to the obstruction in Hochschild cohomology to lifting a $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ -scheme $\mathfrak{X}$ along the map $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle/v_{1}^{2}\to\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ (and even along the map $\tau_{\leq 2p-3}j\to\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ , where $j$ is the connective complex image-of- $J$ spectrum). For instance, the first $k$ -invariant of $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle/v_{1}^{2}$ is given by the map $\mathbf{Z}_{p}\to\mathbf{Z}_{p}[2p-1]$ defined via the composite

$$ \mathbf{Z}_{p}\to\mathbf{F}_{p}\xrightarrow{{P^{1}}}\mathbf{F}_{p}[2p-2]\xrightarrow{{\beta}}\mathbf{Z}_{p}[2p-1], $$

where $P^{1}$ is a Steenrod operation and $\beta$ is the Bockstein. In other words, $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle/v_{1}^{2}$ is equivalent to the fiber of the above composite. On the other hand, the extension class for $\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}\to\mathrm{F}^{p}\widehat{\Omega}^{\not{D}}_{\mathfrak{X},0}\to L\Omega^{p}_{\mathfrak{X}}[-p]$ is computed in [Pet23, Lemma 6.5] to be the composite

$$ L\Omega^{p}_{\mathfrak{X}}[-p]\to L\Omega^{p}_{\mathfrak{X}_{p=0}/\mathbf{F}_{p}}[-p]\xrightarrow{{c_{X,p}}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}_{p=0}}\xrightarrow{{\beta}}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}[1], $$

where the “first Sen class” $c_{X,p}$ can be defined using Steenrod operations on cosimplicial algebras via [Pet23, Theorem 7.1]. We hope to explore this further to obtain a tighter connection between the results in this article and those of Petrov’s.

#### Remark 6.

Theorem 2 has the following counter-intuitive consequence: if the HKR spectral sequence for $X$ degenerates at the $E_{2}$ -page, then the differentials in the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence obstruct the lifting of $\QCoh(X)$ to a smooth and proper left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category. In particular, taking $n=\infty$ , the condition in Proposition 3 that $\pi_{j}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p})=0$ for $j\not\in[-p^{n},p^{n}]$ is vacuous; so we find that if $\mathcal{C}$ is a smooth and proper $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -linear $\infty$ -category which admits a smooth and proper lift to $\mathrm{BP}$ , then its Tate spectral sequence collapses at the $E_{2}$ -page.

This was already known if $\mathcal{C}$ lifts all the way to $S^{0}$ ; see [Mat20, Example 3.5]. In particular, therefore, one class of $X$ for which $\QCoh(X)$ does satisfy the hypotheses of Proposition 3 and Theorem 2 are toric varieties; but in those cases, degeneration was already known for $X$ of arbitrary dimension (since they are $F$ -liftable). Interesting examples of Theorem 2 and Proposition 3 are currently lacking, but one would be most welcome.

#### Remark 7.

One could also ask the following question: if $n\geq 0$ , is there an example of a smooth and proper $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category $\mathcal{C}$ which does not lift to a smooth and proper left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category?

The idea to prove Proposition 3 is essentially the argument of [Mat20], so we recommend reading that paper first. Recall Bökstedt’s calculation that $\pi_{\ast}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\mathbf{F}_{p}[\sigma]$ , where $\sigma$ lives in degree $2$ . By [Mat20, Proposition 3.4], Proposition 3 is a consequence of:

#### Proposition 8.

Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a smooth and proper $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -linear $\infty$ -category such that $\pi_{j}\mathrm{HH}(\mathcal{C}/\mathbf{F}_{p})=0$ for $j\not\in[-p^{n},p^{n}]$ . If $\mathcal{C}$ lifts to a smooth and proper left $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -linear $\infty$ -category, then $\mathrm{THH}(\mathcal{C})$ is $\sigma$ -torsionfree.

To prove Proposition 8, we need a preliminary result. It follows from [DHL+23, Theorem 5.2 and Corollary 2.8] that there is an augmentation $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\to\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ ; composing with the map $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ defines a map $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ .

#### Proposition 9.

The map $\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ factors, as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra map, as the composite

$$ \tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\to\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}). $$

#### Proof.

It evidently suffices to show that the map

$$ \tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}(\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}\mathbf{F}_{p})\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}) $$

factors, as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -algebra map, as the composite

$$ \tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}(\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}\mathbf{F}_{p})\to\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}). $$

There is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -map $\mathrm{BP}\to\mathrm{BP}\langle{n}\rangle$ , which defines an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map

$$ \mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP})\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}}\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}\mathbf{F}_{p}. $$

This map is an equivalence in degrees $\leq 2p^{n}-1$ .55 5 For instance, this follows from [ACH21, Proposition 2.9] (see also [Dev23, Remark 2.2.5]), which says that for $n\leq\infty$ , there is an isomorphism

$$ \pi_{\ast}(\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle}\mathbf{F}_{p})\cong\mathbf{F}_{p}[\sigma^{2}(v_{n})]\otimes\Lambda(\sigma(t_{1}),\cdots,\sigma(t_{n})), $$

where $|\sigma^{2}(v_{n})|=2p^{n}$ and $|\sigma(t_{i})|=2p^{i}-1$ . Therefore, it suffices to show that the map $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP})\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}}\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ factors, as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map, as the composite

$$ \mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP})\otimes_{\mathrm{BP}}\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}); $$

equivalently, that the map $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP})\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ factors, as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ -map, as the composite

$$ \mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP})\to\mathrm{BP}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}). $$

Here, the map $\mathrm{BP}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is just the composite of the map $\mathrm{BP}\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ with the unit $\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ . Since $\mathrm{BP}$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{{4}}}$ -algebra retract of $\mathrm{MU}$ (compatibly with their natural maps to $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ ), it suffices to replace $\mathrm{BP}$ by $\mathrm{MU}$ in the above discussion; in fact, we will even show that the map $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{MU})\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ factors, as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -map, as the composite

$$ \mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{MU})\to\mathrm{MU}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}). $$

Here, the map $\mathrm{MU}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is just the composite of the map $\mathrm{MU}\to\mathbf{F}_{p}$ with the unit $\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ .

Recall from [BCS10] and [Kla18] that there is an equivalence $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{MU})\simeq\mathrm{MU}[\mathrm{SU}]$ of ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -algebras, and that the augmentation $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{MU})\to\mathrm{MU}$ is given by taking $\mathrm{MU}$ -chains of the augmentation $\mathrm{SU}\to\ast$ . The ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ - $\mathrm{MU}$ -linear map $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{MU})\to\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is therefore equivalent to the data of an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -map $\mathrm{SU}\to\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}))$ . Since $\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ is concentrated in even degrees, $\mathrm{GL}_{1}(\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}))$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -space with even homotopy. It therefore suffices to prove the following claim: any ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -map $f:\mathrm{SU}\to X$ to an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -space $X$ with even homotopy factors (as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -map) through the augmentation $\mathrm{SU}\to\ast$ . Indeed, $f$ is equivalent to the data of a map $\mathrm{B}^{3}f:\mathrm{B}^{3}\mathrm{SU}\to\mathrm{B}^{3}X$ . Since $\mathrm{B}^{3}\mathrm{SU}=\mathrm{BU}\langle{6}\rangle$ has an even cell decomposition and $\mathrm{B}^{3}X$ has odd homotopy, the map $\mathrm{B}^{3}f$ is necessarily null (so $f$ is null as an ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ -map), as desired. ∎

The proof of the following result is a direct adaptation of that of [Mat20, Proposition 3.7]; it could also be proved using the methods of [Dev23].

#### Lemma 10.

Let $M$ be a perfect $\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ -module such that $\pi_{i}(M)=0$ for $i<a$ . If $M$ lifts to a perfect $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)$ -module $\widetilde{M}$ , then $\sigma$ -multiplication $\sigma:\pi_{i-2}M\to\pi_{i}M$ is injective for $i\leq a+2p^{n}-1$ .

#### Proof.

To prove the result of the lemma, we can assume without loss of generality that $a=0$ . Then, there is a map

$$ M\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\widetilde{M}\otimes_{\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)}\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p}), $$

which is an equivalence on $\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}$ . By Proposition 9, the map $\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ factors through $\mathbf{F}_{p}\to\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ , so we see that $\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}M$ is a free $\tau_{\leq 2p^{n}-1}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ -module on classes in nonnegative degrees. Therefore, $\sigma$ -multiplication is injective through the stated range. ∎

Proposition 8 is now a consequence of the following, whose proof is a direct adaptation of that of [Mat20, Proposition 3.8].

#### Proposition 11.

Let $M$ be a perfect $\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ -module with Tor-amplitude in $[-p^{n},p^{n}]$ . If $M$ lifts to a perfect $\mathrm{THH}(\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle)$ -module $\widetilde{M}$ , then $M$ is free.

#### Proof.

The argument is the same as in [Mat20, Proposition 3.8]. Indeed, $M$ is a direct sum of $\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})$ -modules which are free or of the form $M_{i,j}=\Sigma^{i}\mathrm{THH}(\mathbf{F}_{p})/\sigma^{j}$ (see [Mat20, Proposition 3.3]). Since $M_{i,j}$ has Tor-amplitude in $[i,i+2j+1]$ , the condition on $M$ implies that $M_{i,j}$ could appear as a summand of $M$ if and only if $-p^{n}\leq i\leq i+2j+1\leq p^{n}$ .

The class $\sigma^{j-1}[i]\in\pi_{i+2j-2}M_{i,j}$ is killed by $\sigma$ , so taking $a=-p^{n}$ in Lemma 10, we see that

$$ i+2j>-p^{n}+2p^{n}-1=p^{n}-1. $$

In particular, $i+2j+1>p^{n}$ , which contradicts $i+2j+1\leq p^{n}$ . Therefore, no $M_{i,j}$ can be a summand of $M$ , so that $M$ is free. ∎

In the remainder of this note, we will clarify the relationship between liftings of $X$ itself and Hodge-de Rham degeneration. First, observe that assumption (b) in Theorem 2 is only a condition on $\QCoh(X)$ , which is essentially why Proposition 3 is the more natural noncommutative statement. It seems to me that assumption (a) in Theorem 2 could be removed if we asked that the structure sheaf $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ itself lifted to a sheaf of ${\mathbf{E}_{{2}}}$ - $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -algebras.

One could ask about lifting $X$ itself as an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -spectral scheme in the current setup [Lur17] of spectral algebraic geometry. Unfortunately, this question often does not make sense, since $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ is generally not an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring [Law18, Sen17]. Nevertheless, the question does make sense if, for instance, $n=2$ (since $\mathrm{BP}\langle{1}\rangle$ is an ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring). In this case, requiring that $X$ lift is significantly stronger than the assumptions of Theorem 2, as shown by the following.

#### Proposition 12.

Let $X$ be a smooth and proper $\mathbf{F}_{p}$ -scheme. If $X$ lifts to a $p$ -adic flat $\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}$ -scheme $\mathfrak{X}$ , then the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence for $X$ degenerates at the $E_{1}$ -page.

#### Proof.

The lift $\mathfrak{X}$ defines a lift of $X$ to $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ via $\mathfrak{X}_{0}:=\mathfrak{X}\otimes_{\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}}\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ . It suffices to show that $\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ admits a $\delta$ -ring structure; then, the Hodge-Tate gerbe over $\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ (from [BL22b, Proposition 5.12]) splits, so that the conjugate (and hence Hodge-de Rham) spectral sequence for $X$ degenerates. The fact that $\mathfrak{X}$ is assumed to be flat implies that $\pi_{0}L_{K(1)}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}\cong\pi_{0}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}}$ . By [Hop14], if $R$ is any $K(1)$ -local ${\mathbf{E}_{\infty}}$ -ring, then $\pi_{0}(R)$ admits a $\delta$ -ring structure (functorially in $R$ ). Globalizing, we see that $\pi_{0}L_{K(1)}\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathfrak{X}_{0}}$ has a $\delta$ -ring structure, which implies the desired claim. ∎

#### Remark 13.

It follows from Proposition 12 that lifting an arbitrary-dimensional $X$ to a $\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}$ -scheme suffices to conclude Hodge-de Rham degeneration; in particular, this assumption is significantly stronger than those of Theorem 2. One intermediate between the assumptions of Proposition 12 and Theorem 2 is the following: one could assume that $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ only admit a lift to a sheaf of ${\mathbf{E}_{{m}}}$ - $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ -algebras (whenever this makes sense). Proposition 12 corresponds to the case $n=2$ and $m=\infty$ , while Theorem 2 roughly corresponds to the case $m=1$ (and $n$ arbitrary). What constraints does such a lifting impose on the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence for $X$ ? For instance, if $p$ is an odd prime, and $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ admits a flat lift to a sheaf of ${\mathbf{E}_{{2n+1}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}$ -algebras, then the general construction of power operations (following [Hop14]) along with the equivalence $L_{K(1)}\mathrm{Conf}^{\mathrm{un}}_{p}(\mathbf{R}^{2n+1})\simeq L_{K(1)}S^{-1}/p^{n}$ of [Dav86] shows that $\mathfrak{X}_{0}$ has a lift of Frobenius modulo $p^{n+1}$ . In particular, if $\mathcal{O}_{X}$ admits a flat lift to a sheaf of ${\mathbf{E}_{{3}}}$ - $\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}$ -algebras, and $\dim(X)<p$ , then [DI87] implies that the Hodge-de Rham spectral sequence degenerates for $X$ .

#### Remark 14.

Finally, one might wonder whether a lifting of $X$ to $\mathrm{BP}\langle{n-1}\rangle$ , or $\mathrm{ku}^{\wedge}_{p}$ , or even the sphere spectrum can be used to prove that the HKR spectral sequence degenerates. Unfortunately, it seems that there is no clear relationship between HKR degeneration and liftings to the sphere. For instance, the stack $B\mu_{p}$ over $\mathbf{Z}_{p}$ lifts to the $p$ -complete sphere spectrum (by writing $\mu_{p}=\spec S[\mathbf{Z}/p]$ ), but the HKR spectral sequence for $B\mu_{p}$ does not degenerate by [ABM21, Theorem 4.6]. Nevertheless, there are some liftability and torsion-freeness criteria, such as those described by Antieau-Vezzosi in [AV20, Remark 1.6 and Example 1.7], which do guarantee HKR degeneration.
